div.p: GOLCRIVOT McDOUGALL'S PATENT SELF—RAISING FLOUR THE EXA MIN ER, FRIDAY, JUNE 22 1900
" Yes, bqt they affect our faith." cnnnot help that. MIA f. s
"But do you not think you should know some- thing of the beliefs of our Church before saying that which condemns them."

"I really don't wish to speak about this," said Duncan, "but I suppose I must defend myself. I confess that I am ignorant concerning many of your ceremonials but I know something of your beliefs and the history of your church. It may seem like boasting to say so, but I have read scores of books on the growth of your Church. Indeed, hr six years Church history has been a favourite study of mine." "But your histories have been written by Protestants, I suppose? " "Oh, no. I have read both sides." "You have read Catholic histories by Catholic' historians?"

"Oh, yes," and he named several authors. , "And yet you remain a Protestant ? " "It icepends on the standpoint from which we look at things, doesn't it? Believe me, I have no wish to foist my beliefs on you." "Oh, you could not." "I daresay not. But look, yonder is Boggart's Clough." "Yes; I shall be able to find my way easily from there."

"You will at least allow me to accompany you as far as your lodge .gates, Miss Neville? I shall have to pass them 'myself, and' it is rather dark, although the mist has lifted somewhat." She thanked him coldly and walked by his side silently. "I suppose your house was built in. the fifteenth century?" be went on presently. "Yes; at least the old part of it was." "It has a history, I suppose? It was the scene of some stormy deeds at the time of Hairy VIII." "Yes, I suppose so. But what is that light? "I think it must be the light at your lodge." "Yes, it is. lam very glad. It is kind of you to walk with me, Mr. 'Rutland." "And kinder of you to allow me," replied Duncan. "I am afraid you regard me as an unpleasant companion." You must confess that you are an enemy to my faith," she said, impulsively. "None the less, I hope lam capable of being ordinarily courteous," replied Duncan, pleasantly. "I claim the liberty of thinking for myself, but then--surely there's some disturbance yonder? There are several lights, and I think I see a carriage." "I hope mother has not been anxious about me," said the girl.- "I sincerely trust not. Let us hasten on." "What's the matter ? " asked Duncan as he came up to the gates. He heard a lady's voice, but she did not speak in answer to him. "I know she went to Mrs. Crossland's. lam •afraid she must have been lost in coming across the fields. I'll go by the road in the carriage, and you must take the lantern through the fields." There was a hubbub of voices, and Duncan had to speak loud in order to make himself heard. "Is that Lady Neville ? " he said, hurriedly. "Yes," replied that lady. "May I ask if you are looking for your daughter ? "
"'tes, I am quite anxious._ Rave you seen her?"
"I am here, 'mother," said Alizoxi.
A few seconds later the necessary explanations were given, and Alizou sat in the carriage beside her mother.

"I am sure I am exceedingly obliged to you," said Lady Neville to Duncan, graciously. "Will you not ride with us as far as the Priory? You will be'nearly two miles nearer your home. Duncan accepted the invitation; but little was said during'the journey, and the young man was glad when he found himself alone again. "At any rate," mused the young man, as he sat in his study-chair that night, "I have been intro- duced to the principal Catholic family in the district."

The next morning, as he opened the Lynfo: Observer, he saw a prominent announcement to the effect that Father Sheen would give a series of Sunday Evening lectures on the Catholic Religion, and would answer some of the allegations made against his Church. "Whew!" exclaimed Duncan as he read. "I see an exciting time in the future." For several Sunday nights the congregations at Tudor Chapel were much thinned, while the Catholic Church was crowded to excess. Duncan read the reports of Father Sheen's addresses with much interest, and noted the letters which challenged him—Duncan—to answer the statements which the priest had made. Father Sheen's lectures concluded amidst a flourish of trumpets, while Duncan made no sign whatever. The truth was, ho was loth to enter into a wordy battle. In some ways he longed for thefight. He noted the weak points in the priest's armour and saw how easily his arguments might be answered, and yet some power held•him back. Presently the townspeople began to laugh freely, and some spoke to him rather jeeringly on the subject. "We thought yo' 'ad more grit in you, mester," said an old weaver. "If Luther 'ad bin like yo' .we'd 'ad Popery wi' us naa. I tell yo', yo're noan Lancashire."

"No, I'm not," said Duncan. "But what would you have inc do?" . . "Answer him from Tudor. 1;:f what you said t' first Sunday nest is true, then your duty is plain." Ile walked out of the town and presently reached a footpath across some fields. His mind was very active, and before he realised what he was doing he had sketched a series of addresses which he knew would destroy the arguments of the priest. "But.l'll not give them," he said to himself, as be wandered on. "I'll not give them " ; but he could not tell why he had come to this decision. Presently he looked up and saw Alizon Neville coming towards him. He had neither seen nor heard anything concerning her since the night he had accompanied her across the moors, He had often thought of her since then, and had wondered if they would ever meet again. He went towards her with quickened step, and almost held out his hand. She in her turn nodded coldly, and passed on without a word. He was disappointed, and yet he knew no reason why he, should be. Ile had no right, to expect, because he had rendered her a simple service, that She' would treat him cordially in the future. Besides, she bore one of the oldest names in Lancashire. She was a daughter of one of its most important houses ; it was natural, therefore, that she would treat him, the minister of Tudor Chapel and an enemy to her faith; with, coldness, if not disdain.

"I must get back to my work," he thought. presently, and a. little later sat before his desk. Ile took up his pen to write a sermon. This, however, was the document which he produced: , "To tho Editor of the Lynford Observer. "Sir,--As I do not think it would best serve the interests of truth if I followed the example ot Father Sheen, and gave a series of addresses in nr-s church, especially as many Roman Catholics woula not, or dare not, enter the building, I shall be happy to fall in with the suggestion made by "Truth Lacer" in Wednesday's issue of your paper. I therefore invite Father Sheen to a public debate of three nights' duration, to be held in the Industrial Hall, on any dates most suitable to him.. I would suggest that a comsuittee of twelve gentlemen, of which half shall be Protestant and half Roman Catholic (although the Roman Catholics do not number a tenth of the population) be formed to arrange proc e' eedin,vs. I am perfectly willing, moreover, that Father Sheen shall select three 'such enhjects as he regards to be essentially Roman Catholic as the topics of debate, and thus we shall be able to publicly discuss, on neutral grounds, those great. issues which cleave the Church in twain. Although I have never uttered one word against the Roman Church, per se (the corre- spondence in your paper and Father Sheen's addresses having arisen out of broad general principles which I enunciated), I would submit the following topics for Father Sheen's consideration : "1. Was the Reformation and the consequent growth of Protestantism, a Necessity? "2. is the doctrine of Papal Infallibility in accordance with the teaching of Scripture, or history, or reason?
private indgment in matters of religion right or wrong?--Yours faithfully, 461)micAN RUTLAND. "

On the following Saturday the editor printed Dlincan's letter in large type, heading it with the words: "A Challenge to Father Sheen." A leading art il€' was also given, supposed to be impartial, while many suggestions were offered. Before the dey was over the reiigious element in the town was in a state of greal. excitement. "All." said the young Protestants to the Catholics, who had been calling Duncan a coward, "we shall see who's th' coward now " ; while all sorts of surmises were offered as to the probable result of the letter which had been written. And thus Duncan Was led, by forces of which he

div.head: .LADIES- LETTER:
div.p: .LADIES- LETTER:
MY DEAR NELLIE,

Of dresses in general there is plenty to be &lin just now, for at every turn one is confronted novraies, m.2st of them 'more or less bmaxtiful. Some in the new materials " Eventzkil ' and " Fantail " especially pleased me. The gauty, light material is to be had in many exceedinsly pretty colours. The " Eol:enne" crtlpe comes in tones of grey and fawn, and it is greatly in demand. There are also nem: Organdie inualins with their fresh summer colours and their pretty floral stripes. For river meetings and house boat parties scarlet foulard is being very much A costume of this materiai with lace iichus and broad scarlet satin sash tied. at the side struck me the other day as being altogether charming. The silk front was filled in with lace, and there was also a lace-edged flounce. The sleeves were in full folds at the bend of the arm, while at the elbow was a small tuft of drooping lace let in under the folds of materials.

A useful bathing dress had the tunic and blouse in one, with separate knickers left loose at the knees, hemmed up under a band of braid. Tho top at the back was gathered and put into a band which buttoned under the side. The small vest was stitched in each side of the neck with the collar, a band of binding making the inside neat. The collar was of white serge with coloured trim- ming. The blouse was sown to the tunic round from the opening on the right side to the front, then after fastening the bodice down the band was taken over to the side where tato strap, with buttons, made a finish,

some particularly attractive specimens of head- gear are obtainable just now. One that I saw the other day was of white crinoline with rosettes of wl-ite tulle and white feather jetted down the centre. Another was a Tuscan straw with black feathers and pink chiffon mounted on wires, with rosettes of chiffon under the brim. A very charm- ing hat was open-fronted and was rliade of fancy straw with a large blue silk poppy at the side, darker blue wings and white plumes. .ft is scarcely necessary to tell you. that the varieties of chapeaux are almost numberless. They present a wide field for the exercise of skill on the part of the milliner, and this season some of the results obtained are very beautiful. The chiffon ruffle has come quite to the front. far the prettiest are the white ruffles of enor- vinous width, and edged with pleated black gauze, net or ribbon. Some ruffles are exactly the shape and size of the feather boa, gradually decreasing in size and tapering off to a point. Others form 'simply a huge Pierrot ruffle, with flat ends of .eliffon, adorned at intervals with gathered pom- pons. One entire width of chiffon is gathered up to form the end, and here the newest accordion- pleating is employed, as the chiffon is only lightly fastened with stitching and retains its shape to the last. The ruched ruffles consist of innumer- able strips of chiffon, set in close treble or fourfold box-pleats. Some are made of crimped or pleated strips, closely gathered and sewn to the centre of a narrow ribbon, and the fulness in and out in cas- cade fashion, and v.;,;,e,lit down imperceptibly to the ribbon.

It has been very rightly observed that the chief interest of the toilette of a woman of fashion lies in all the little accessories which are required to complete it. Amongst the latest novelties which I have seen were charming sunshades painted by hand in bold designs and mounted on fancy sticks with bows of satin ribbon at the handles. Amongst them were some which had purple irises on a black or white material. Sunflowers or clematis, con- volvulus or nasturtium lend themselves admirably to this decoration purpose, or wild flowers may be chosen. Very brilliant results are obtainable from such contrasts as poppies on a green sunshade, or yellow iris on a blue one and corn flowers on one of a yellow shade or orange. For a child nothing can be more becoming than a simple frock of muslin or sonic other inexpensive washing material. A lovely smock of China silk was shown to me the other day. It was elaborate- ly embroidered with white silk in an Empire bow design, both on the front of the dress and on the collar. The sides and sleeves were smocked with white, and there was a frill of silk at the bottom of the skirt, edged with fine white Valenciennes lace, and feather-stitched with silk at the top. A larae Leghorn hat was worn with this, which had a wide, drooping brim, and was trimmed with white ostrich feathers. It had ribbon strings, which tied under the chin. A pretty white dress was made of fine book muslin with a yoke and sleeves finely tucked and trimmed with transparent lace insertions, and there was a deep frill of lace edging at the bottom of the skirt. This was worn over a slip of soft blue silk, made quite separate, so that the muslin dress could easily be washed and got. up, and round the waist there was a belt and bow of blue silk. A charming hat of rustic straw was worn with this, which had a tucked blue chiffon lining in the brim, and was trimmed with bows of sc ft blu,N ribbon and clusters of pale pink roses.

It will not surprise you, perhaps, to know that the blouse is as popular as ever, nor need one wonder when it is borne in mind what a number of neat dressy specimens it is possible to proeure for a comparatively modest outlay. The latest designs Jan be copied in any ordinary colour of the moment, and thus it is within one's power to provide a stylish bodice to match a skirt with but little trouble. With silk skirts most useful to wear are the pleated brilliant blouses, with trans- parent yokes of lace, and these are charming in blue, white or other pale coroucs, with flounced skirts of Oriental satin or China silk. A white gown can be formed in the same manner, with the blouse and an unlined skirt of some semi-trans- parent fabric, or showing transparencies of lace, Which can be worn over coloured slips.
Your loving JENNIE.

div.head: "WOMEN'S CHAT."
div.p: "WOMEN'S CHAT."

Mrs. Gladstone was said to have alone nasde the Glynne famhy famous, but she is not the first of its ' members to find a last sanctuary in Westminster Abbey, as a grand niece of John Glynne. who was a fam us Cromwellian, was laid there in 1733. Something lik three thousand bodies are supposed t) have been buried within and around Westminster Abbey, and of these, about one hundred 't'ere women. Many bore famous names in hi,tory. Lady Palmerston is buried there under precisely similar circumstances as led to Mrs. Gladstone's burial in the Abbey,instead of at Hawarden. re Ceeit's,and the Percy's,amoug other leading families, h ave also laid same of their women there, but in all probtesility Mrs. Gladstone will be the last woman to find a sepulchre within the precincts of Westminster Abbey. Hawarden Castle, where Mrs. Gladstone was born in 1812, and which was her hom9 during the long peril(' of her life, now passes to her grandson, William Glynne Charles Gladstone, who is a boy at Eton, fifteen years of age. The estate was purchased by Sir John Wynne in 1602, and the old castle dates back to the time of the ktlitens. Sir Stephen Glynne, the father of Mrs. Gladstone, was the eigbth baronet who succeeded to the property and he died in 1815, when his daughter Catherine was a little girl of three. The property passed to his son, then eight years old, another Sir Stephen, who died unmarried in 1874. He settled the property upon his eldest nephew, the late Mr. W. H. Gladstone and his heirs, witu the provision that Mr and Mrs. Gladstone were to ,have the use of it for their lives.

Mrs. Gladstone had eight children, four sans and four daughters, and three sons and three daughters sur.ive her. Mr. W. H. Gladstone ber eldest son, died in 1891. and it is her only son Master W. G. C. Gladstone, wno now succeeds to the Hawarden property. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone also lost their little girl Jessie Catherine, who died in 1353 at the age of five. Tbe sec md sou is the Ray. S:ephen Gladstone, of Hacvarden, and the othsts are Mr. U N Gladstone and Mr. Herber.; Gladstone, M P. Vine eldest daughter is Mrs. Wickham' the wife of the Dsan ot Uncoln, and Mrs. Drew and Miss Helen Glad- e:one are her sisters. _ =_ _

The widowed Coanteso of Airlie has been stayine with Ledy Reber a at Bloemfoeteio, where she WAS receatly nursing her husband. Lord Airlie, on of the finest soldiers in the Army was foremost in the fighting at the Moeder, 4.nd at Brandfort, where he was wounded in , the (4133 w and he had only shortly resumed comineed of his regiment, before in e was kided near Pretoria. The Countess of Airlie, and Viscountess Cranblree are sisters, tee daughters of the Earl of •Arran. Since Lady Airlie has neea is Seith Africa, her family of six entitle wadi- ren have been staying at Beurnemouttnani her son Lord Ogilvy, be now euceeeds to the earldom, is only re gen years o'cl, the same age as his cousin, the Hon. Robert Cenii, who will in all protiability be one thy Marquis, or pollees the Duke of Salisbury. 'lwo years ago, Lard and Lady Roberts were the guests of the Earl and Countesa of Airlie at Co t achy Castle in Scotland, one of the family seats of the head of the Geityys. Toe Castle is muppesed to be haunted be the ghost of a druiemer by, who, having given seme offence, was tied up in his drum, and thrown from the Castle walls. Before he died, he said his ghost would haunt the family for ever,and for centuries the roll of his spectral drum has scared the inmates cf Cortachy Castle. Again and again it haa been heard and within a week coals member of the family has been stricken with death. It was not however heard whets the father of the , late Earl of Airlie died, iind there does not seem to be any authentic testimony that the spectral drum was sounded before the death of the gallant soldier, who has , just lost his life in South Africa. Sir Therms Lipton is understood to have ben in treaty for the teaancy of Inverary Castle. Tho eheot- ' ings, which extend to about 14,000 acres, are let separ- ately, and belong to Mr. Nix, but soon after the death of the late Duke of Argyll', the Castle and grounds were advertised to be ltt, and it would be quite in accordance with modern tradition, if they were taken by some millionaire like the popular provision merchant. The ever vowing activity of wom,n in oublc and political affairs, finds ample evidence in the many meet- ings and congresses held during this month. The list ,includes discussions upon politics, the Cnurch, temper- ance legislation, social questiouses.uch as over-crowding, old-age pensions, education, factory reform, besid -8 many others affecting the welfare of the people. Were tt not for Parliament, it would almost app-ar from the tarp number of gatherings, that women are now taking the principal part in the discussion and furtherance of these questions of public interest. Miss Lawson it is interesting to note, takes the same view o! the Temper- ance question as her distinguished father. She would have all or nothing. That epirit however has led to nothing but the wasted efforts of half a century, and if any progress is to be made with this problem, temper- ance reformers slanald abandon it for the principle of 'taking what they can get from Parliament and asting for more. There are nearly 14 000 women on the Post Office staff and nonstant addi ions are being made to the number. Partly for this reason it has been necessary to extend the buildings of the General, Post Office in London. The Prudential Insurance Company, which is almost entirely staffed be women clerks, is else making vast additions to its head office in London. There,every accommodation is made for the cornice and convenience of the girls, even to the envision of a garden and pro- menade en the roof of its immense buildings. In small numbers women are employed at the Bank of England end at Messrs Rothschild's. Ia America, there is a news- paper, entirely managed and produced by women, hut even in this country there is hardly a business or a pro- fession in which women are not taking the same places as mete in the various walks of life. Wide strings of gauze, chiffen, muslin, or tulle, appear on almost every picture hat, and not always t the wearer's advantage. Strange as it may seem, very few women can wear strings of this description but it is the mode, and that is enough. One needs a picturerque face, and a picturesque gown, to indulge in strings suc- cessfully, and these should be loosely pinned en one shoulder, both for c felness and effect. • In Paris, it is possible to send a blouse, shirt, vest. jabot etc., to be " laundried," and receive it hack again in an hour or sten procedure our drese.ers, wile frequently take a week or ten des sto get up the simplest or such articles, would do well to note, and copy. We are fre- quently hearing of distressed gentlewomen who appear to be unable to find remanent lye emreornent. Surely here is an occupation, and an opening ready to their hand. Never were laces and lawns more worn than at the present time, and dressers wile would retort the work promptly, skilfully and well done, could easily secure as many customers as they could ('ea' with. " MADGE."

div.head: MYSTERIOUS DROWNING CASE AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE MYSTERIOUS DROWNING CASE AT WARRINGTON.
A Cattle Dealer's Sad End.

Wycliffe Society's Annual Meeting. The annual meeting for the election of officers and the transaction ot other business in connection with the Wycliffe P.S.A. Society was held on Sun- day afternoon. The president (Rev. J. Youge) occupied the chair. nig REPORTS. Mr. B. Farrar, the secretary, in submitting the 7th annual report, stated that in some respects it fell below Previous years ; in other respects it was quite equal,but in many respects far ahead of anything previously re- ported. In numbers the membership was below last year, in interest and efficiency, the meetings had been equal, whilst in the special efforts put forth they had surpassed.auything previous'y reported. In this latter respect he more particularly referred to the successful mission held in March by Mr. Cairns, the P.S.A. Federa- tion missioner. The meetings had been kept up to a high spiritual standpoint and they 'mete thankful that many of the brethren had been able to testify for Christ. They were indebted to many willing hinds and hearts in carrying on their work, and they now acknowledged toe services which had been so efficiently rendered. The brotherhood had been visited during the year by death, and had lost very useful members by the deaths of Messrs. W. Smith, John Wood and John Fowler. Some of their members had gone to South Africa and they were thankful to have received good news of them. Thee hoped soon to hear that peace had been drc'ared ' and that they would shortly be able to give their friends a hearty welcome home. The report proceeded to refer to the mission held in the church by Mr. G.R. Cairns, of Ceicago. During the mission 70 declared for Cnrist. Senreof these had joinei other churches and many had joined Wycliffe church. He thought it was fitting that some reference should be made to the sudden death of the Rev. J. K. Nuttall, of Great George-etr eat P.S.A. Society at Liverpoel,who was their friend and consellor. He had forwerded a letter of sy:npathy to the secretaty of the Great Georef -street Seniety. The year closed with an enrolled membership of 614 with an average attend- ance of 310 It was a m Ater for regret that their membership had fe,creasee, but there was nothing to make them despondent. There was much to in them more earnest and faithful in their work and to endeavour individually to work up the membership of the society. Daring toe year 694 nrlzes had been gained 349 in the first six month s and 345 during the eecene. Thssa together with previous years made a total of 7,199 books. The sick club was doing its work qu'etly and well, and at the close of the v.ear's work a setisfactory division was made to the in fletters. The m'm.hlitshile of the society was 41.6 for the first three months. In con- clusion he pleaded for deeper interest its the welfare of the P.S A. Mr. Mills presented the absentee visitors' report and Mr. Hawthorn. toe Benevolent Fend statement. After meeting the claims on tee fund there was a balance in hand of 193. 31. Mr. Wuetnall subinleted the report of the temperance committee, showing that 15 pledges bad Wee taken during the year. Mr D maid Reeves' report cf the sick club showed that there were 80 members and the work was progressing satisfaetoril C. Th ClllliteteN in moving the adoption of the reports, referred te the present position of the s iciety, and stated that wnile the membarehip was not as large as it used ti be there was much to encourage them. The Wycliffe P.S.A. Society had been an unsoeaka.bie bles- sing to a great number of men. Ho had received tributes from individuals as to the good thee had received by attending the meetings. Despite the fact that many similar aeencies :lid been started in Warring- too since the Wycliffe Society was inaugurated, theme were still many vu me fellows and men who were to be seen walking the streets on a Sunday 'afternoon, and would he all the better if they could be brJueht under the influence of their society or others in the town. He would ask them to assist the offieers in increasing tee membership. Mr. HEALEY gle,,lndei. and the reports were adoptel,

div.head: ' A SOLDIER'S DISCHARGE.
div.p: ' A SOLDIER'S DISCHARGE.
The Melancholy End of his Meritorious Career.

"'Tie a bad job. I love the army, and yet I have to le aye it." The man was doleful, and with Rood reason. For close upon six years—" the happiest time in my life," he sighed—Harry Rogers had served his Queers and country in the Army Medical Corns, and had c-imei to r gard his career as absolutely honnd up with that of Tommy Atkins. But disease—'hat dreadful enemy, Coneumptien—ovatook him, and he was pronounced " einfl: for further service." Concerning this dashing of his hopes to the wall, Mr. Rogers spoke freely to a reporter of the South London Press, who saw him at his residence, 31, Calais-road, Camberwell, London, S.E , recently. He stated : "For three years aid two months I did duty at Malta and Orate. A fine time did we have in Maltasand a busy eventful time in Crt te ! I was sent to rho latter island with the Army Medical Corps during th-. international occupation. We had the Seaforth Highlanders and the Royal Welsh Fusiliers to look after, and the enervating, fever-iafecting climate made the sick list a tremendous one, prrticularly among the Welehmeu. I had not been there long before I meselt began to get rather' dickey,' and was sent back to Malta, where I remained in hospital for three months. I began to feel th-re was something very wrong with me, and when I saw from tee visitiue medical man's ticket that Consumption was my enemy, I did not feel very hopeful lot the future. It was with eurpriee, therefore, that I received the news that I was to be tianeferred to Netley Hospital. It was early in JanuarY. 1899, that I arriveat Nttley. aad on the last day of that month I received tin melancholy notifice- twit mat I was discharged, • troth for service,' on a pension of sixpence per day." 1 " And yen again entered upon a civil life ?" " Yes ; hut I looked a pitiable olject. I was Ithoreughly b oken down, with fever lurkine in my !system and a persist,nt coueh night and day. I was as weak as a rat, and my condition was mule worse by heavy perspirations that c3notantly w. rried me at night. I would wake up simply drenched. Everybody look-d at me %ith pity, and I fully believed my days were numbered—at any rate, that I should be of very little use in civil life. One day,however, I in' t a friend whom I had not seen for six poste. He was quite upset at the change in my appearance. I told him all about my troubles. He said, "Look here,Harry, I have found oat something which lies had a wonderful effent upon me ;" and he mentioned the name of Dr William,' rink pile for pale people. I listened in a half-hearted sort of way. fair, having been mixed up with the Medical Corps so intact), I had not n:uch faith in ares thine not prescribt d by the doctors. Ant how, my friend was a man in whrm I had gre it car& lence : I knew that he was not the men to speak at random. To tell you the truth, I went right away and ho sem. of Dr. Williams' pink pill?), and c-immenbed to take therm" What Waq t he off =ct ?'' " For fourteen days or so I (I'd not nitice much irn- provenser.t, hut then I beLtan CO feel a decrease in toe irritating, racking cough. Sleep also rain to me rno,.e readily at night, mad in the morning I awoke refreshed and ready for work. It beget) to dawn tr ion me that it was the pflle that were doing me en much goo I. I had, great hopes; I continued to take them, ;ant by rlevree,, my t.trength returned, my nerves grew steadier, and the dierea.ing perspiration which s') ,ttain overtook me entirely disappeared. Then I went out in the op. n a,r took long walks, and begad to experience the real de lights or revived treneth and buoyant spirits to !retch I had so long been a s ranger. f" When I came +tut of the hr,spital I w ietied b %rely Be'. Recently I form imy weight hail Roue up te 103% Besidrs this t,kini'-n if flesh the bloom of health. hair returned to my cheek, the cough has gone, an I I feel as fit 'as anyone could ever teel--th inks to Dr. Williams' pink pills " For the rest, Mr. Rotors, who is a L ambeth man horn arra tired. ha. no greater wish than tiaat soff,-I,r, 1-k himself should know of his experience, and he consent I to there d4tmils being ruhtisnen.

div.head: (copyright.) THE TEMPTATION OF DUNCAN RUTLAND.
div.p: (copyright.) THE TEMPTATION OF DUNCAN RUTLAND.
BY JOSEPH HOCKING,
Author of "The Birthright," "Mistress Nancy Molesworth," "All Men are Liars," "The Story of Andrew Fairfax," &c.

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS: Alizon Neville, who belongs to an old Roman Catholic family, pays, for curiosity's sake, a secret visit to Tudor Chapel, the Nonconformist place of worship at Lynford. She hears the new minister, Duncan Rutland, and by chance is thrown across his path.
CHAPTER 111.
Wily DUNCAN CHALLENGED FATHER SHEEN TO A PUBLIC

div.head: DEBATE.
div.p: DEBATE.

"It is very kind of you," said the girl, after hey had gone a few yards together. "I am glad I happened to be coming this way," said Duncan. "I hesitated at first about crossing the fields, and almost repented that I did not keep to the road; now I shall regard my decision as exceedingly fortunate." The girl made no answer, but walked quietly by his side. Presently her foot caught against a huge stone which stood in the path, and she stumbled. "Pardon me," said Duncan, "but could I render a further service by offering my arm? " "Thank you," said the girl, and she accepted his offer.

The young man realised a pleasant sensation as she placed her hand upon his arm. The night did not seem at all dark or dreary now, nay, rather he was glad that the darkness made the girl dependent on him.

"You know the neighbourhood well?" she asked presently. "Yes, I think so," said Duncan. "I have cnly just come to the district, but I have spent a good deal of time on these moors. They are very fine, and they help me to do my work." "You are the minister of Tudor Chapel, I think you said_? "
- "Yes." "Then can you work so far away from your church? "

"Yes, I work out my sermons on these moors. They inspire me to think, and—and somehow they make my world bigger, and life less sordid." "But you cannot read on the moors? " "I could when I first came; we had a fine September, you remember, but I do not care so much about reading for a month or two. I did nothing else for six years, and it is a relief to me now to rest my eyes." , "But you are fond of reading ?.," "Oh, yes, naturally." " Why_naturally ? ' .. . . .

! "Oh, 'I suppose a minister is bound to be a bookish man. Besides, this is supposed to be a bookish age." Duncan Rutland was not sure, but he had an idea that the girl who walked by his side wat, she for whom he had opened the lodge gates at Neville Priory that morning. He had learnt, too, that her name was Alizon ; this he fancied was her Christian name, for he knew that it was of Lanca- shire origin, and he had never heard of it as a surname.

"I suppose you are fond of reading, too ? " he said, in order to keep the conversation going. She had not told him who she was, and therefore he felt a difficulty in speaking freely. "Yes, I suppose so ; but you, as a minister, would doubt les3 regard my reading as light and frivolous," she said, laughingly. "I suppose all your books are very serious? "
no. I read anything, everything, from Descartes to Dumas, from Sir William Hamilton to Sir Walter Scott."
"Do you read Dumas in the original? " „_.. ..
"Yes:"

The girl felt more at ease with him now. She had found a subject in which they both were interested. "Do you read Dumas? " asked Duncan. "Yes, no—that is, I did, until--". She stopped suddenly, and did not finish the sintence.

Naturally Duncan did not press his question, ut he could not 'help wondering at her words. "Of course, some do not like French novelists," he went on, trying to make matters easy for her, "and Dumas described phases of life alien to our English ideas. Still, he was a groat master of romance. Indeed, for pure romantic writing, he was in some respects superior to our own Sir Walter. It goes without saying that you have read "The Monastery" and "The Abbot ? ' " No. "
"No! I pity you, or rather, I envy you. I would give something not to have read either of them. Let me recommend you--" "No, I shall not read them." She spoke rather Curtly.. _
said the young man, curiously_ "No. The truth is--of course it is of no interest to you ; hut I am a Catholic." , "Oh, 1 understand."
• "You may have heard my name, at least, my mother's name, Lady Neville; I am Al izon Nevi lie."

"Oh, certainly. How foolish lam not to have thought of it. The young man felt in a somewhat awkward position. He remembered that Lady Neville was the representative of Catholicism in the district, and that he had been spoken of as an enemy to the Catholic faith.

"I suppose," he continued presently; "that we are at the opposite pales in thought." "I suppose so," she replied, somewhat curtly. ' For a time there was an awkward silence. frer words had placed a barrier between them, and the young man did not know how to break it down. "Your's is a splendid old house," he said presently. ."I like old houses. In fact, I like old things generally. There is generally some mystery surrounding them, and romance." "Yes, I like old things too," she replied, "even in the world of religion," she added, somewhat awkwardly. "So do I," said Duncan, heartily. "I like old churches, and I 4e visiting old monasteries and convents."

He wanted to "set her at ease, and he had no desire, nay, he felt it would be unkind, to discuss religions matters with her. She, however, was young and enthusiastic, moreover, she was excited. She was thankful for his company across this dreary part. of the country on a dark night, but she could not help feeling somewhat strange at the thought of walking with a young man whom she regarded as an enemy to all she had been taught to hold most dear. Without weighing her words therefore, she began to argue with him. "if you believe in an ancient religion," she said, "is it not strange that you should be the minister of a modern sect? " " Von do not Wish me to answer you, Mss Neville, do you ? " he asked, with a laug,h. "It might be interesting if you did." she replied. "Well, then," said Duncan, "if I went to live in an old house, I should most likely have the place newly drained, I should lighten the dark ruuns, I should remove all possibility of disease. It would be the same house, only purified." "You mean by that, that you believe in an ancient religion: but that it is freed from--" _ . -

" Excute me," interrupted Duncan, "but had we nra better change the subject? 'Believe me, I hold at religious convictions as sacred. If your religion your deepest needs---" "It does," she replied, hastily.

"Then, let us say no more about it." "But you are an enemy to my faith. You have attacked it in your chapel. I beard you—that is, I have read—the—the papers. -Father Sheen told ma--" Again she stopped awkwardly; she had siil more than she had intended.

"I have heard that Father Sheen is a very good man," said Duncan, again trying to help her. "Ile is, indeed; the best man I know. I wish you knew him ; I wish he could speak to you about —the thin!rs you condemn." "It would give me great pleasure to meet Fat lwr Sheen," replied Duncan. "You know nothing about the Catholic Church, I expect," she continued presently. "No ; that is I know little of your ceremonials, and your 'services generally." "Then why do you condemn them ? " 'he felt she was scarcely polite in continung to press tbic subject, but the circumstances of their meeti,4, caused her to act with less than her ordinary caution. _Besides, she felt that she limit defend her faith in the presence of its enemy. "I don't think T ever hare," replied Duncar.. "As far as I know, I have never mentioned the ;'..otnan Catholic Church since I came to Lynfor. I have simply dealt with what seems to me ink. aurtant principles."

div.p: naa never oreamt, towards a path which changed the whole trend oc his life.
"Father Sheen 'll noan tak' thee up," said a man to him as he passed down the stravt that night. "Yi, but he will," said another. CHAPTER IV.
HOW DUNCAN'S LETTER AFFECTED FATHER SHEEN.

Father Sheen sat in' his study on the morning on which Duncan's letter appeared in the Lyn/ord Observer. He had performed his offices in the church, had afterwards eaten a good breakfast, and had now come into his study for a little quiet. "I've had a busy time," thought the priest, "and now I'll have a rest. Those addresses cost me a world of anxiety and labour in spite of all the help I could get. But they are over now, and, that young. fellow has not shewn fight. Well, l'inf glad I gave them. I shouldn't be surprised 1 they result in converts." He sat down before the fire, and saw a copy of the Lynford Observer lying on the table by his side. "More letters, I expect," he thought. "I must say I am surprised that young Rutland has never written a word. Well, all the greater victory for me. I shall now be regarded as a champion 0Z us, Cause."
A minute later he sat with his mouth open and his eyes staring into vacancy. At first he could not believe what he read, but presently he saw that, there could be no mistake about it.

"Bother it," he cried, at length. "I never thought the fellow would do this. At the worst I thought he would only answer me in his own chapel. But a public debate, a public debate!" He perused Duncan's letter through again very carefully. "I therefore invite Father Sheen to a public debate of three nights' duration, to be held in the Industrial Hall, on any dates most suitable to him," he read aloud.

"I suppose I must accept," he said, piteously, "although Heaven knows I am not prepared for such work. I wish I'd never meddled with the business. I shouldn't, either, but for Lady Neville and Alizon. Yes, it was Alizon who was always at me." There could be no doubt about it; Father Sheen was much worried. He paced his room many times, constantly giving expression to savage ejaculations. "P.m not the man for the work," he said, "I've done but. very little reading on those lines for many years. I've forgotten my Greek, while even my Latin is rusty; as for Church history, I am all at sea. I'm an old man, too, while this young fellow is fresh from six years of training. I'll refuse; I'll say I haven't time, I'll refuse to dis- cuss the doctrines of the Church with an heretic."

All this did not satisfy him, however, because he knew it would not satisfy the public. To say that Father Sheen had a bad half-hour after read- ing Duncan's letter, would be to very inadequately describe his feelince.

"It's all Lady Neville's fault; yes, and Alizon's," he said, at length. "They got me into this scrape, and they ought to get me out of it. I'll go down to the Priory; that's it. 1 know her ladyship's at home. She will help me out of it." This decision evidently gave Father Sheen con- siderable relief. There is always comfort in the thought of being able to shift our burdens on the shoulders of others, and when, as a few minktes later he made his way towards the Priory, he felt quite jubilant at the thought that her ladyship would help him out of his dilemma. "Well, Father Sheen," said her ladyship, "I am honoured this morning. It is not often you come before lunch, except on special occasions. I hope nothing's the matter." "Plenty's the matter," said the priest. "I wish to speak to you on a very important matter this morning." "Come into the library. There's a good fire, and no one is in the room but Alizon. You don't mind her being present, I suppose ? " "Oh no, on no. it has to do with Alizon as much as with you." "That's right," said her ladyship, leading the way, and wondering what caused the woebegoL. expression on the old man's face. Alizon met Father Sheen with a bright face as he entered, and bestowed on him a look of genuine affection.

"Father Sheen wants to see us both this morning, Alizon," said her ladyship, pleasantly. "I hope you'velnot been a naughty girl," she added, with a laugh. "Oh, no, nothing of the sort," said the old priest, hurriedly. "Have you read—that is—have you seen ?—but I suppose you haven't?" "Seen what?" asked her ladyship. "This morning's Lynjord 01,server." "No, I haven't." "Then, here—read this, your ladyship," and he put the paper in her hands. Lady Neville began to open the paper. "Excuse rae, let me find it for you," said the old priest, hurriedly. "Ah, there it is—that letter, signed Duncan Rutland. It's an awful business, isn't it? " - - -

Lady 'Neville read the letter, and then with a smile passed it on to Alizon. "What shall I do? " asked Father Sheen. "There's only one thing you can do." "What? " • "Why, accept, of course." - "But I can't. I—l—that is, I'm very rusty on such questions." "Then you must furbish your weapons. My library Iva' be at your disposal. The letter is perfectly fair, perfectly courteous, you cannot refuse. You would be the laughing-stock of the town if you did." "Do you think so?" "I am sure you would. You see, you gave those addresses."
"I did, I did," said the old man, ruefully. "You persuaded me, you and Alizon, to give them. I wish I hadn't.,

"Why, you told me they had been well received." "Yes, they were, ,or they seemed so, but a public debate, your ladyship, a public debate!" "Nothing could beletter. You are, of course, sure of your arguments? " "Perfectly, oh, perfectly." This he said in such a plaintive way that her ladyship could not help laughing aloud. "Then what is there ti) fear? You are not a youth of twenty-six, you are an old man, and a skilled debater, all the arguments for our faith must be perfectly familiar to you. "Your ladyship is very kind." "Not at all. lam simply wanting to shew that this is a most fortunate occurrence. You will be able to speak to a Protestant audience, you will be able to shew them the truths of our faith, and make them realise how foolish they are to keep out of the Church.. Why, you might begin a New Reformation movement in the town." _

"Yes, yes," said Father Sheen, tamely. Lady Neville was partly in earnest, and partly joking in what she said. Belonging as she did to an old Catholic family which had suffered mi for faith's sake, she was a good Catholic; she did not believe that any arguments which Rutland might adduce would do harm to her cause; at thw same time she doubted the powers of Father SheeL, While believing in the sacredness of the priest's offices, she regarded many of the priests very lightly as men. In the past, many who had come to the Priory to say Mass, were not even invited to par- take of food with the family, but had to be content with the company of the butler, or, at best, the housekeeprr. Since those days custom had changed, and she now treated Father Sheen with respect, but she had no exaggerated notions as to his powers as a debater and scholar. She was sincere in her belief that he would triumph in argument, but she could not help laughing at the thought of the old man appearing as an intellectual gladiator. The gift of humour is very dangerous to a religion built on ceremonial. Lady Neville did not realise this at the time ; nevertheless, she felt a strong curiosity to know what Duncan Rutland would say. "Of course, all the Catholics would have to be invited to come," sighed the pripst.

“Of course.” _ _ - "Don't you think it will be very dangerous? That young _Rutland is a clever fellow." "But you will be there to answer him. Think of the•tritunph of pulverising him." "Yes, yes, of course." said Father Sheen, sadly. "Of course you *ll come and sit on the plaiform ? " "If you wish it." "Oh, I do, I do! But, but don't you think it would be better if 1 got one of our ree,gnised speakers to accept his challenge? " "No, certainly not." "Why?" "Because the people would assume that you are afraid, and because the words of a stranger could not have the same weight as yours.* "You think not? "
"I am sure of it: Basides, if you invited one of our recognised debaters, Rutland would be justified in doh's, the saute thing. No. no.. you are the

man. Besides, when you have beaten him, al' promotion for you as a consequence. It may ea°. , in a Bishopric." "Oh; I am delighted!" Alizon broke ita triumphantly; "it is glorious, Father Sheen," eh.' cried. .1 "Of course, of course," said the old rug* gloomily. "When will you begin? " she asked. "I 211/1. afraid it will be impossible before Christmas." "Yes, yes," said the old man, eagerly, "it be impossible before Christmas. It must take coy siderable time. I shall have to spend much do' in reading." "In reading! Why? " "I must prepare myself." "But you have been a priest for-fortY Are you not always prepared ? " "Yes, yes, of course," replied the old ras "Besides, the longer you delay the matter, tll4 longer time this Mr. Rutland will have to prepare' I do long for you to give •him a good thrashing' He is a conceited fellow."

"Is he? How do you know ? " "Oh, I met him once," and Alizon described beg journey with him across the moors. "And what did you think of him, Liao Neville? " asked the old man, eagerly. "Oh, he seems a smart fellow. He looks all 3 speaks more like a lawyer than a dissent minister. He is the very opposite of the aprfie., type. But for the fact that he is clean-s he has a certain military air. He is young. gerl'e° manly, and I should say decidedly good-looking* But such fellows are seldom strong as debaters. Father Sheen shook his head. be "Well, what would you advise me to do? - asked. "Oh, I should write to the paper saying that'll accepted Mr. Rutland's offer." "Yes, what then ? " he asked, plaintilell.; "Really, Lady Neville, I am not the man for WI work." a "I should fix, say, January 10th, 17th, all, 24th for the debate. Those are early ciciairli; nights, and the people will be able t come crowds." c‘c,f course, of course," said the old man, but if/ his heart he prayed that the hall might be era "Then I should name six of our most reoloc`-d Catholics to act as a part of the committee, leave them to arrange details."
" Yes. "

"That is all, I think." "All except the subjects." p t" "Oh, yes, the subjects. Well, do you is those which he has suggested? They strike nie he, important. If you prove your case on the lines, II - marks out, Protestantism crumbles to the gronne, • "Oh, quite. Crumbles to the ground," and to! of old man repeated the words in a lugubrious to", of voice. write

Oh, it is fine!" cried Alizon. "Let us the letter now, Father Sheen. Ido long ,to see before it appears in print!" Half-an-hour later the letter was written, approved of. Alizon was jubilant, Lady Ne."'- confident, Father Sheen in despair. rte. The following Wednesday Father Sheen's le -rrif appeared, and a few days later arrangements "", the debate were made. All the town was ferment. and on the night of January 10th, doors of the Industrial Hall were literally besi egeb, more than an hour before the time announced for t debt to begin. (To be continued.)

fact he felt perfectly sure that with the whole of the meeting the resolution was a foregone conclusion. They had cline for the purpose of carrying it and he did not suppose there was a single dissentient in the whole of the audience. They hoped their friends in Monmouth would get their Sunday closing. Of course it was never right to "count their chickees before they were hatched" and it was not at all safe to conclude that becalm the measure had succeeded in being read a second time in tbs Reuse of Commons thet it would pass out of the House of Cemmena. A numher of things might arse that would be clisaierous to the passing of the measure. They had also to remeneb.r that supposing it passed through the Lower House it did not follow that it vess going to get through the Upper. Tney knew what fre- quently happened to measures of that kind when they got in the remarkable atmosphere that seenel to 111 the Upper House--(laughter)—and seeing that the Prime Minister was cynieal on all matters of temperance re- form, for which they were a'l intensely sorry there was ' pessibly the danger that Monrneuth might have to wait ' a little longer yet. Seeing that Monmouth strongly askel for it and seeing that the centiguocs principality of Wales rejoiced in the possession of a Sunday Closing Set and that Sunday Closing was a success wherever attempted, in Scotland, Ireland and continental coun- tries, the day could not be far distant when not only Monmouth but the whole coultry cf Eaglend would rejoice in that great accomplishment. (Applause). The upholders of the trade were themselves very much coucerned about the Monmouth Bill and one writing to a Licensed Victuallers' organ said it was really a serious thing as if Monmnuth get it because it happened to be next to Wales why should not Gloucester which was nexe to Monmouth get it in the following Session of Parliament and so tho whole measure might be carried hit by hit through the House. Amen so let it be. (Applause). They were all prepared for that glorious consemination, and ghould be delighted when it came to pees. As , regarded the Sale of Drink to Children Bill he thought it was a bill that appealed to their sympathies very powerfully. He had been pleading in his church te-day for collections on behalf of the Indian Ramine fund. Especially that morning he dwelt upon the sufferings of children in India and he had very good reason to believe that the very respectable amount they collected was laxg,ly due to the strong sympathy felt by the parents when they heard about the terrible sufferings of little children. He hoped they were prepared that night, in fact he felt confident that not only they, but the country as a whole was prepared to accept that measure which sought to keep temptation out of the way of the little children] woo were at present so terribly exposed to it. It was sitisf ectory to note that although no mown.° had poised the House of Commons touching the question there had been certain movements in that direction already with considerable success. Three years ago the bench of magistrates in Liverpool took measures to check the Sale of intoxicants t )children under 13 and they had done so with the best posit:it:, results. Buriningharii took a similar step last year and the bench of Birkenhead had also done so with like precious results. In Franc, Hungary, and Belgium similar results followed, and heavy fines and penalties were attached to any infringe- ment of the regulation in those continental countries. Theyemerkeble thing was that all this had been done in the towns and countries mentioned without anyone being hurt by it. Seine raised objections and said that by means of passing the measure they were infringing on the rights of parents, end chat parents ought to be at Perfect liberty to send their boys and girls to fetch their beer, but was it not a tact that the State had already stepped in to protect the children against the paren-s. (Hear, hear). Was not that the case with regard to the Factory Acts, a great many years ago, when little child Ten were sent at a terribly early age to work long hours in mills and factories, and also in mines. The State stepped in and said " You must not 8 ibject your children to this cruel tyranny" and the children were delivered. It was precisely the same humanitarian feelieg that had in- spired them to endeavour to bring about a time when parents should not be allowed to send boys and girls to public-homes on the ground of the danger and tempta- tion to which children were exposed. EP hoped that not only they in Warrington bat their fellow countrymen throughout thelaed would support the measure. One of the reasons that these nee° lags were being held in summer was in order that their Senators in the House of Commons might knew that the country was watching the business with great earnestness and eagerness and that the feeling of the country was that the children should bs saved from the terrible temptations. He hoped the result of that meeting and similar ones would he that when the matter came before the Committee in the coming weeks they would feel that it was not a matter to be trifled with, postponed or whittled away, but a inetter to be carried through to a triumphant issue. (Applause). Rev. T. BISHOP supported, and expressed regret at the tiseuce of the Rev. Li. G. Et inercs Continuing, he glee, he was a strong supporter of temperance in all its branches. He had been a teetotaler for something like thirty years. and he was thanxful to see- that his chil- dren had been teetotalers from their birth. As he was coming along the streets, a few minutes be!Pre he entered that hall, he saw a little girl carrying a bottle full of beer which she had just fetched from the public-house and it made him feel very sad to think of that little girl becoming so early acqnainted with the inside of a public-house. He said "God save our chil- from that." (Hear, hear.) Thee wanted the people of Begland to become sober and they could ouly do that by saving the children of to-day. Then the men and women of to-morrow would be s-ber. Tney were told that the wages of the country were thrown away in drink and that the business of the country was steppe on acceuntetif drink, and that its prosperity was, if riot actually waning, at a standstill because of the drenken habits of the pennle. Amoneet other naticna it was a by-word that an Eigtishman swears and drinks That was the character he get and it was only too true of many he (the speaker) had seen when he had been abroad. He had seen them and had been sorry to have to own that they were Englishmen. Would not England be more prosperous if the people were more sober? As regarded Sunday Clo4nre lie thought it was very essential. He wished all public- houses were closed on Sunday so that the lonblicens could have a rest and that they and their familioe eeu'd come to the House of God to worriip with others. They were now debarred from doing sea because they were compelled by law to open their bowies and serve cue— tomers. Many of them desired that the bow,: should be closed bylaw. In some of the towns he hid been connected with a pn'l had been taken and the inhale- tents were asked " Do you wish for Sunday Closing,do von vote against it, or are you neutral ?" Trio over- whelming in jerity, something like 80 to 90 per cent. was in favour of the public-houses being closed on Sun- day. (Heel., hear.) if the people wanted the houses to be closed on Sunday why should not they be closed ? (gear, hear.) People talked about robbing the poor man of his beer. That was a phrase invented by the Devil. He did not believe a Christian man invented it and the man who did was not a philanthrepier. Com- paring the amount of drunkenness in Warrington with that in Jersey (where he was born) the rev gentleman said he bad seen more drunkenness in Warrington in a Imonth than he saw there in 21. years. He did not think Ihe ever saw a woman drunk in Jersey. They must

remove temptation from the people: He asked them to join in prayer to Gt)d for the passing of the bills, tor as the late Poot Laureate said "More thino lre wrought by prayer ' Than this world dreams of.' The resolution was ply, to tee meeting and carried with one dissentiAnt.

_ The Rev. E T REED then moved that the Chairman be requested to sign petitiene in support of the Bill and send copies to the Marquis of Salisbury, the 11,ght Hon. A J Balfour, M P., Sir Matthew White Ridley, Bart. (Home Secretery), Sir Henry Campb-11 Bannerman, M. P. eat d the member for the Borough. At the outset he offered his coneratulations to the Chairman on his appointment to the Preeitiency of the Temperer c Federation. He sincerely hoped that during his term of office he would he the =Atte of promoting greater intere:t in the temperance cause in the town After hav- ing lived there for a little over eight years, it seemed to him (the speaker) that there was still a very great need for greater effort by the Christian people of the town in the direction of stemming the evil of lot ,mperance. He hoped Mr. Powell's advent to the Presidendy of the Fedeiation would lead to a great increase of interest in every part of temperance reform. He understood tnet some years ago Mr. Powell held an important position in connection with the Church of Englwd Temperance Aseoclation in the Diocese of Newristle His (the speaker's) frame was in that DiooB4B and he himself held a similar ones for about a couple of years in the Diocese of Durham, that of organizing secretary. It would appear that Mr. Powell was posee.seed of the knowledge which a man who held the pe.ition to which he had been elected shozild possess, and he trusted that therewould be great progress in the future in this town. (Applause.) So much had been said about th 3 Sunday Closing Bill that it was quite unnecessary for him to add anything more. Some years ago a very earnest effort was made in the county of Durham to obtain Sunday Closing end the Bill passed through the House of Cern- mope and was read a secnni time in the House of Lords. It was overthrown eotirelyehe was sorry tO say, through the influence of the Marquis of Salisbury. He hoped that fate would not befall the Bill, which had for its object to obtain Sunday C:osing for Moornoteh. As regarded the Sale of Drink to Children Bill it delighted him te find a few weeks ego that such an important body as the Manchester City Council passed a resolution by a large majority in favour of the Bill, and he understood that more recently the City Council of Liverpool passed by a large majnr,ity a similar resolution. (Applause.) He was of the opinion that such resolutions as these would have far more weight with the House of nonemons than any number of resolutions passed at meetings like the present one, not that he wished to minimise the importance of the meet. ing. The Government would give more att(ntim to resoletions passed by public mien:opal boeies than they would to these passed at meetings of that character. As to the nature of the 8.11 no words of his were necessary. The rev gentleman proceeded to read the letter of a ! publican who was of opinion that children should not be sent for intexieating drink. He (the speaker) yielded to no one in his intense love for hiellcenritry. The truest patriot was he who desired that those who dwelt in the lard'ehould be living upright lives, tin: he must confess that since his visit to Canada some years ago he had often felt ashamed that the mother country was An behind her daughters. Mr Bishop referred to his experiences in Jersey. During seven and a half months' residence in the capital city ot Canada he (the speaker) never saw a drunken woman and he did not see ten drunken men. Public-houtes and hotels, RO far as the sato of drink was concerned, were closed on the Lerd's Day. Hs never saw a child in the streets without shoes and stockings. As one who love] his own country deeply and strongly he felt ashamed that England set such an example to her Colonies. They set us an example because in most of our Colonies and Dependencies there were laws in existence prohibiting the sale of drink to children under 15 or 16 yeare of are The Rev. W. H. DRUMMOND seconded. Undoubtedly the question was one wlalch affectsd the laity quite as much as the clergy. There was an impress'oe that clergy and ministers were fond of agitating an I wanted to restrict peoole and rob them of their pleasure, and i all sorts of disagreeable things for sinister reasons of their own. Whet these reasons were he had be?n unable to disc aver. Re should Ilk to have had as the secender of the reeolntion some worldly minded, sensible layman to show that the laity was interested in the question. He

1-1-a;4l-vva-greerl--with'the Chairman that it tifas unneces- sary to say mirth about the Children's Bill. No doubt those who hal studied the question very closely and had gone into the terrible and heartrending details connected with it were absolutely convinced that it would be a good thing. There were however a great num• boy of people who never gave a thought to the question and it was that great mass of people they had got to make reaFze in some degree the great evil aid the terrible social danger of the previa practice of sendiog children to the public-house. People who had not studied the question. who had not come into actual contact with the evil, tiaid it was very much exaggera- ted, and that it would be a very considerable aojal and family inconvenience if children were not allowed to go t o public-houses. That kind of thing was said in a very plausible way. They had got to convince those people, who did not want to be convinced, that they were face to face with a terrible social danger. From his own obtervations ,nd from what he had heard, he was convinced after studying the qaestion very closely, that they could do a great deal to check the tortilla growth of drunlten habits amongst the people by keeping all children up to the age of 16 years out of public-houses. He thought it was one of the most im- portant que•tions before them at the present time. , Un- fortunately the English dem cracy did net sufficiently realise the need of the Act and a meeting lik that could do a great deal to gain public opinion. He was not at all sanguine that they shoal get the Bill out el the present Parliament. He should like to make a suggestion that when their local memher next addreesed his consti- tuents, they should very severely heckle him on the uestion. (Laughter.) They might not agree with him politically or with his temperance progromme but they were his constituents and had a perfect right to ask hi it !questions as to his particular views and policy on that point. Members of Parliament were squeezable and they might get the member for Warn?' on te pledge himself to vote for the Bat. Mr. WILLIAM Rohmers proposed a vote of thanks to the Cnairman f,)r presiding and to Mr. Broil& for his services. _ _
_ Councillor ELLISON sesonded. The motion was nria.nimoasly carried. Tne CHAIRMAN briefly responded and the meeting termina.tel.
