div.head: BAZAAR A'-40 FETE AT
div.p: BAZAAR A'-40 FETE AT
WALTON LEA.
The Ragged School Cause.

A vsit to Walton Lot I-lard-us has usually been associaued with Mr Grostield's generosity in allow- ing the general public to view bis fla_. collection of ' flowers, but last Thursday those who visited his beautiful grounds had aiyther object —an 1 a still more wormy 011e—ift view. Chis was to help the Varriugton liagged Sula, ay School Mission in their efforts to tree that illSqt.tillol of a debt which has been incurred in the purchase ot the buildings in Bank--street, now used for the purpose of the Mis- sion. Ihe splendid work of the institution is so well known amongst the inhabitants of the town that it needs no word of commendation here. Its object may be stated in a sentence. The work of the :Mission,' say the promoters, "is to spread the principles of truth, temperance and cleanliness, especially among the young." It is, then, an in- stitution eminently de-crying of support—certainly one whose beneficent operations should not be per- mitted by the wealthy to be hampered tor want of sufficien,-, money. _ _ _

The Ragged school was establishel about 12 years ago by Mr. James Skellaud, who was helped by a band of Christian workers to fled out and get together the poor ragged .waits and gutter children in Warrington, some of whom swore orpr;ans and all destitute, of the influences that are so needful to help them in the way 0: lite. For some years these children have, in large numbers, met-, together in a room in DaHam-lane, on Sunday afternoons, where they have been nurtu.ed and taught to sing and read Bible lessons. in the evening a Mission serr ice has been held, where they were taught to fear God, by men who with grea*, self-denial, gave themselves up to the work of trying to 'rescue the perishing." In addition to the Sunday services, they have a drum and tiro hand which practices twice e week, a choir practice and a girls' sewing class weekly, and they are trying to establish a cookery class. There is also a good Band of trope and a god Templars' Lodge in connection with the school. During the past year, clothing has been supplied to Sjale 200 children, and 30 fatherless girls have been fitted with new boots and over-all pinaforas. Recently new pte,oiisea .we.re purchased—the old Couoty Court, Bank has been coasiderably altered and renovated. Na ftlor;.-, heating apparatus. cooking arrangements &c,, have been put in,and a large warm water bath ia the b,sement, so ',hat the children may nave the luxury of a bath once a week. All this has meant, of course,A large expesditure.with the result tly,t previous to last Thurslay there was a debt of £5OO on the buitdinz. The Mayoress and other philanthropic ladies were anxious to clear off the debt, and eventuallF decided upon a bazaar and open-air fete as a means of freeing the scho,Jl of its ny..metary burden. A number of gentlemen were coarynarideered t) assist them.

Th work of preparation was-begun as qu,ckly as pos- sible and energetica!ly puriued, and on Thursday the bazaar and fee was opened by the Mayoress in the beautiful grounds of Walton Lea, kindly piaeed at the ,iisoosal oftile promotora by Mr. and Mes Crosileld. The bevy thunderstoren of the morning had made all con- cerned apprehensive, but long before the time for commencement the weather had cleared,and the proceed' lugs throughout the day and evening were conducted under the urv,t agreeable atmoThweric conditions. There was a Uir attendance of people fr.-.rn Warrington and tile neighbourhood who were able to appreciate to the full the delightful natural surroundings in which the pr-iceedings were conducted. There wa.s a large attendance at the opening cere- mony, which took place in thelmziar tent,the audience 13, log cimposed in:alio?, of fair ladiel. Tne gentlemen pre,ent iocluded the Rev 1 Yonge, Mr R T Faircloogh, Mr Leonard Davie, Mr E Lloyd Joretn, Mr J Fairhurst, and Mr Jarne,Slrelland.

Mr. LLOYD JONES ',aid they were sorry to announce that Mr Arthur Croetield, who was to have presided at the opening ceremony, was unavoidably detained in London. The Mayor had requesteci that the Rev John Yonee should take his place, and he (Mr Jon-s) had great pleasure in asking Mr Yonge to preeale over the gathering. (Applause.) The Rev. John Yonge having taken the chair, the Gitana Ladies' Choir gave their first coatribution—the parr song " Ash Grove," which was very well sung. The threrustee said he much regretted that Mr Arthur Croefield was unable to be with them on that occasion, as he would have ably filled the position which lei (the speaker) had been called upon at such !short nr!tice to occupy. It so baPeened toe, he understeol. that their friends the clergy of Werriaeton were all ,ngaged at the funeral of the late Bishop cif Liverpool, and so they also wore unable to attend the opening cere:nony. He felt quite sure that the clergy were fulfilling a duty and a privileee in peeing a last tribute of respect to a good mars and a good bishop, who did so much while he was the episcopal ruler of the diocese of Liverpool to endear himself to the hearts of fellow-Christians of every denomination, They were all agreed. he supposed,teat the Ragged School wee a drsira.ble institution to eupport, and he thought all of them were disposed to agree that the Ragged School of Warrin,gten had se far been useful mad had done good service. (Applause.) Tney believed, also, that it was capable of being still further developed and made more useful sell to the Tyler and fleet-cited children, of we-in, unfor- tunately,there were so many in the town of Warrington. Tee Rigged Selo I was of an undenemlnationel descrip- tion, and he thought happily so, because if there was one work in which Christian people of all classes and kinds coul.l heartily combine surely it wee the work of trying to lift up from the uneappy conditions of life of the ragged childeen of the town those who might perhaps, under Christian influence, and the influence of kindly sympathy, prove to be in future resneetitele members of society, heeding useful and holoura.ble lives. (Applause) That was the object tee Rsgereel School lead in view, and he was sure their desire would be that, by the bleesing of Ged, 1113 school might be more and more instrumental to that end in the days that were to come. The object of the le cziar and fete, as they knew, was to dispose of a debt of something like -2500 which was stid remaining on the premises. Tense premises, he believed, had a somewhat curious history. He understood that they began by being a Wesleyan Methodist Chapel. Afrerwards, being deserted by the Goseel, the premises fell irr:o tile nende ef the Lew, and were used for some years as the County Court for toe district. Then the Law severed its connection with the building, ancl it had come back to a certain extent into the hands of the Gespel. They all trusted that by means; of those premises great gee I would long continue to be done in Warrington. He had much pleasure in asking the Mayoress of Warrington to open the bazaar. (Applause.) Time MAYORESS said she felt that she, too, almost ought to apologise tor the position she found herself in that day, as no one regretted the absence of LACIV Brookes mere than she did. They hal heard from Mr. Yonge what the needs of the Rageei School wer., but she would like to say one word from a womares and a Mother's heart to plead the cause of the institunion. ,She had visited the school on several ecsasions at the invitation of Mr. Skelland and Mr. Sparks, and she woull like to clay that she had ire 41 &Halted on those occasions with the behaviour of the children. They were attentive and obedevat. and she thought they were well cared for by their good friends the ',eiders and tetschers of the school. (Applause.) She was quite .certain they were all glad in some way to help to make the lives of th re poor child- ren brighter. and one way in which, they Could help was by removing the debt which rested on the building, so that the work might go forward more efficirnqy and fleeeessfollr. See was also very anxious that the f be should be a great saccess because she should like them all to show Mr. and Mrs. Crosfield hsve meets they eppreciated their kineltrees in placing those beautiful grounds at the dispesal of the promothes. (Applause.) Sse wished them all not only to enjey themselves hut te spend their inoner genereuslV, so that their treasurer might ha on Saturday night in the possessien of a sum sufficient to ply off the debt resting on the Ragged She had now great pleasure in declaring the bazaar and fete open, and in wishirie it every possible success. (Applause.) Mr. FAlRutrasy said he had rxtreme /Ye score in nro. pesine a vote of thanks to the Meyoress for having performed the opening ceremony. He hoped her wish would be realised. They had many ready''helpers and he believed there was plenty to be sold, so that all they wanted now was purchasers. He thought that if the outsiders would do as much as the workers had done there would be no reason to regret the holding of the fete and bazaar. (App/suse.) Mr. SKELLAND, in !seconding the proposition, said that some 13 yeare ago, when the Ragged Sitiool was started he never expected to see such a large number of ladies assembled to help them on with their noble work-. The eominittee of the Ragged School desired him to convey their grateful thanks to the ladies and gentlemen who bad so kindly come forward to promote that bazaar and 'ate and to assist in the work generally. • (Applause.)• The motion was enthusiastically carried, and the Mayoreee briefly returned thanks.. ' The attractions on Thursday included the Birkenhead Gitena Larliee' Chair and Mandeline hand, who, under the conduc'orship of Miss Maggie Evans. contributed a excellent self cion of vocal and instrumental music. Then there w,.re a cycling gymkhana, " Aunt Sallys," l a shooting gallery, " striker !and lifter," strength testers, and a tent in which Miss M Balharry,. of Waterlro, displayed her knewledge of the art of palmistry. Moreover there was dancing, that most popular of all forms of recreation, the music being I supplied by the Warlington Bsrough Band, under the conductorship of Mr. Griffin. The refreshment and tee teet was under the management of Mr and Mrs Powis (Town Hall.) The Cycline Gymkhana opened the evening's proceed- . ings,for which a reduced price of admission was cha- ged A fairly large gathering of spectators, mostly of the fair

sex, surrounded the spacious lawn et the front of the house, and on the greensward the various iternB of the gymkhana took place. "Gymkhana" is a very compre- hensive as well as somewhat unintelligible word, and pretty nearly anything in the sports or recreative line can come under this designation. On Tnursday the events of the gymkhana numbered • seven, and very entertaining they were. There were twenty- four competitors, twelve ladies and twelve gentlemen, the names being as follow : •The Misses H Broadbent, 'f U Crosfield, Mabel Fairciough Madge Fairc'eueb, Molly Fairclough, Mabel Henshall, Nellie Henehall, Ethel Lyon Whittle, D3ra Picton, Ethel Roberts, K Picton, and Clarice Walker ; Messrs James Carter, Harry Fairclongh, Lionel Fairclough, Richard Feirclough, jun., C H Bond, Harold Kirkconnel, T Houghton Owen, J T Picton, Forster, Howson, A J Sherwood, and E V Walker. The events included :—Tilting at the Ring, in which the competitors rode in a circle twice rouod ; six stan- dards with rings were fixed at equal distance in the circuit. There were therefore 12 rings at which to tilt, and the competitor carrying off the largest numleer of rings was declared the winner. Arithmetic race : Six gentlemen started from the starting post and rode straight across the lawn:earrying an envelope containing a grocery bill ; at the °tiler end of the lawn there was a lady opposite each competitor ;,the gentlem n banded the bill to the lady to work out, add up the amount, re-enclose in the envelope, seal up the enve- lope, hand the envelope to the gentleman who then raced back to the winning post. The competitor , arriving first will a correct bill was the winner. Tnread-needle Race : Six ladies started from the starting pest each carrying a needle and a piece of teread ; opposite each competitor was statiouea a gentleman to whom the lady rode and handed the needle and thread ; the gentleman threaded the needle and gave it back to the lady and the first lady arriving beck at the winning post with threaded needle was the winner. Slow Race (Ladies) : Owe acresi the lawn; the last one in, winning Apron Race : Six ladies started from the starting post and rode across the lawn each carrying a large linen housemaid's apron ; opposite each competitor was a gentleman, to whom the lady rode, dismounted and dressed the gentleman in the apron,neatness of the bows c-eintine in the juoging. The lady then remounted and rode back to the winning post, the gentleman muslin:: alongside. The first lady arriving with gentleman exactly abreast winning. Coat Race: Six gentlemen divested themselves of their coats, the coats being taken to the far end of the lawn and rolled up in a jumble; the comp.titors rode across the lawn, dismounted, each to find his own cost, turn the same wrong side out, put it on and race back to the winniog post. Needless to say much amusement was caused by the conic events, and the crowd heartily enjoyed the fun. The Mayor officiated as judge, and his awards for the aggregate number of points were as follows : Lerties, Miss Roberts Ist, Miss Mabel Thnshall 2nd, and Miss Nellie [pushed! 3rd ; gentlemen, Mr Forster Ist, Mr Rowson 2nd, and Mr James Carter 3rd. The prizes were afterwards presented to the winners by the Mayoress

In conclusion we must not omit to mention the names of those who worked indefatigably in connection with the event. They are—Ladies' BAZ lar Committee ; The Mayoress (president), Mesdames Armitage, Carleton, Gornall, Tarbuck, Willis, Broadbent, Crosfi,ld, Munro, J L TunA4U, Wright, A Browne. James Fairelough, J Charlton Parr, Sharp, and J Yonge, with Mrs John Fairclough as hon. treasurer, and Mrs Joseph Buckley and Mr E Lloyd-Jones as hon. secretaries. Owen Air Fete Committee : The Mayor, Messrs J Buckley, L Fairclou,gh, E Lloyd-Jones, W H Pigot, J C C H Bond, R Garnett, B S Nowcombe, H G Roberts. C H Wood, H Fairciough, R W Hannah, J T Picton, and R M Roberts, with Mr John Fairhurst as hon treasurer. Mr J Sutcliffe as hon secretary, and Mr T U Spinks as assistant hon secretary. The first clay's proceedings were completely successful, and were evidently thoroughly enjoyed by all who vi.ited the grounds. The receipts handed to the Borough Treasurer as the resul: of the first day's work amounted to £llO. Some money received for the sale of tickets has yet to be added to this sum.

div.head: Closing Day's Proceedings.
div.p: The Closing Day's Proceedings.

There was a disappointing attendance at the hsz tar and open-air fete which was opened for the second and concluding day on Saturday afternoon. The weather was threatening in the early part of the afternoon and this to some extent, accounted for the small attendance. The Mayor (Alderman Roberts) pre-i fed at the openine ceremony and Miss Trude. Crosfield declared the proceed- ings open. The MAeon sell it gave him very great pleasure to be present and take pai t in the proceedings, ere of all becaase the object for which the fete was being held was in itself so intrinsically good. They knew verb well that the ministers and clergy and Sunday School teachers of Warrington were in their respective spheres doing a vast amour tof good and having a splendid in- fluence in the direction of the moral and religious teaching of the young of the town, but outside the de- nominational influence there were unfottanately a large number of children for whom very little provis'on had hitherto been made, and if it were not for the institution in whose interest they were met together he was afraid those children's future so far as their moral and religious teaching was concerned would be a very poor one indeed. If they were not disposed or hid not the opportunity to do that teaching and give that assistance individually which they perhaps might do the very least they could do WAS to assis-, pecuniarily those who were by their self-sacrifice end individual effert,devoting themselves to the welfare of the children. The institution was, as they knew, in very considerable debt, and the fts-,e was being bold to remove that debt if Possible, and it not possible at any, rate to lessen it considerably. If anything could possibly add to the pleasure be lead in taking part in the c.rrmony it WAS that the fête was being held is the gardens of Mr. Crosfield, and that his daughter was taking a leading part in the opening ceremony. The name of the family was one that was honoured above many names in thsir ' town, and bad been for a long time a hoosehoid word in connection with every hing that had made for the good of the town and district. (Hear. hear.) He hopes, that for many generations to come the name might be associated with everything that was gooi and beneficial in the district in which the family res.ded. He had now great pleasure in asking her to open the fete. Miss CROSFIELD sad she was sure they had all been interested in hearing about the Ragged School and son wished it every success. She was very glad to declare the b zsar open. Mr. R. GARNETT proposed a vote of thanks to Miss Crosfield and stated that it gave him especial pleasure to do so. Speaking of the work of the Ragged School he said it was a sort of gutter work which etas not touched as much as it might be, by some of the cuurches in the town. It had been done for a number of years without fee or reward by those in connection with the Ragged School and it was a matter of gratifinetion to know that the clergy of the various denominations very heartily stood by and supported this work. lie was quite sure that as a result of this effort those specially interested in the school would be stimulated to fresh an I renewed efforts for the gool of the town, (Applause.) *rho MAYORESS said she was delighted to have an opportunity of seconding the vote of thanks. The vote was unanimously carried and Miss Crosfield acknowledged the nompliment. The chief attraction of the afternoon was a military tournament which was given by a troop of men of the Earl of Chester's Yeomanry Cavalry under the command of Lieutenant H. M. Wilson, commanding the Arley Troop. Lieutenant Wilson refused to allow three out of the eight entrants to compete because they did not ap- pear in full uniform. As there were only five competi- tors and three prizes for each event, the tournament lost a good deal of its interest. The referee was Lieutenant Wilson, and the judges Sergeant Majors Sauden and Hopper. In the tilting and tent pegging, heads and posts, and lemon cutting Trumpet-Major Yarwood gave an excel- lent exhibition and won three firsts. Being disqualified from winning more than two firsts.the prize in tne third competition was awarded to Private Wright, and Yar- wood took the second prize The prizes in each everft were Ist. £2 ; 2nd, LI 103 ; and 3rd 10s. The results were : Tilting and tent pegging: The conditions in the tilting and tent pegging were: Two rings 2 inches in diameter, 6 feet 6 inches from ground suspended from standards 15 yards apart with peg at end of course. Each competitor to ride at the rings and peeeand to take them again when riding back. Points-6 for a rine,and for a peg " strike "2, " move " 4, " take" 6. Pace— full speed. 1, Trumpet-Major Yarwood :2, Private G H Astall ; 5, Privateli Wright. _ _ _ - - -

In the heads and posts competition, the competitors were allowed three cuts and 3 points with a jump, 10 paces between posts ; 12 pocea oil each side jump ; rings Si- inches diameter; necks inches in diameter ; 6 points tot cut, 3 cuts to the right and 3 points to the left alter- nately. Pace—fair speed. Cuts and points to be properly made. Marks-1 for each cut or point, 8 if all be taken, 1 mark to be deducted if style bad. Two runs- 1, 'far ward ; 2; Wright; 3. Astall. Another item was that of lemon cutting. Lemons were hung from posts 12 yards apart. Cuts 1 and 2 on the right. Pace—full speed.-1, Wright ; 2, Yarwood ; 3, Astall.—A Victoria

Cross competition was a very exciting item, and pro- duced keen competition. The men had to draw swords, jump zeriba, sever head, return swords, oknount,place dummy astride saddle, mount and returh over z,‘riba, Private Astall woo the first prize, Private A, Beckett the second, mid Private Platt the third. Private G.ll. 4%ta1l afterwards give an exhibition of horsemanship, which was receivon 'with approval.

Mrs. John Crosfield presented the pens. A clever exhibition of bicycle trick riding was given on the lawn by Messrs. B. S. Newcembe and W. G. Longdin. The MAYOR announced that Mr. J. T. Baxter, of Lyme], had won the watch competition. The competi- tion was undar the following conditions ;—Tho twelve hours shown by a watch represent 43,200 seconds. Seven hundred and cvreaty sheets were printed each ot which showed the seconds of a minute. The eeconds were disposed of for a penny each. The watch was to be wound, and the second at which it stopped decided the winner. Tne watch was wound by the Mayor. neither he nor anyone else being aware of the time atl which he had started it. It was then deposited in Parr's Bank, and on being examined for the purpose of decid- ing the competition it was found that it bad stopped at 16 ruins, and 24secs. past four. Mr Baxter was the nearest eampetitor, and the watch was accordingly handed to him.

The visitors were entertlined with numerous minor amusements, and the afternoon and cvening were very pleasantly spent. The excellent Viaduct Prize Band from Eirlestown played selections during the afternoon, and la the cvening for dancing:.

Excellent ;rrangement—s had been made by Mr. J. Fairhurst (hon. treasurer),Mr J Sutcliffe (non. secretary), and Mr T U Spinks (assistant loon. seeretarv). The receipts on Saturday amounted to over £BO. The committee will therelore be able to hand over to the ragged school authorities nearly £2OO. We understand that there aro two valuable pictures to be disposed of. and if they are purchased another £75 will be reallwd.

div.head: YOUTHFUL THIEVES AT RUNCORN. Wholesale Larceny. _ _ A Witness Reprimanded.
div.p: YOUTHFUL THIEVES AT RUNCORN. Wholesale Larceny. _ _ A Witness Reprimanded.

Before the Rnncorn bench of magistrates on Monday last, Blanche Welker, a girl of 13 y( ars, and William Bailey, a by of 14 years, were chargee with the larceny of several articles of wearing apparel. Toe facts of the case against the girl Walker, showed that she was in a eituation at Mrs. Elizabeth Sanders, wife of Mr. John Ssn&rs, 54, Ellesmere-street, and at various times she pilfered—three shillings in silver, said to have been taken from her mistress'e pocaet ; two skirts, an antimacassar, five studs, and two handker hiefs, in all value at £1 2s. Several of these articles had been pledged with Mr. William Richardson, assistant at Mrs. Lightfoot's pawnshop ; and with Mr. Samuel Weer, manager at Mr Imisoia's pawnshop. At the first shop Walker had herself pleegei an handkerchief in the name of "Shaw ;" and, at the second place, she had got a womae named Sarah Price, to pledge on behalf of a Mrs Harrison, Duke's Fields, by representing that she had b -en seat by her.— Police Constable George Carringten stated how he had received the girl in custody from a house in Chester, where she bad been taken to by Miss Hinkinson. He charged her with the offence, and she admitted taking 24, which she had given a girl named "Renshaw.' Other inquiries resulred in his recovering the whole of the prop rty, which he now produced. He was, however, unable to find the girl "Ethel Renshaw." —A second charge against Walker, was the larceny of a costume, dress and other articles, the goods of Mre. Sarah Phillip, G:over, widow, of Runcorn.—Walker had gone to Mrs Giover,for the purpose of gel tine a situaticn as a servaat, but Mrs. Glover had replied that she could not leek out for a situation for her unless her father came. Mrs. Glover missed a number of articled about the time the girl used to call, but could not tell where they bad gone.—le was left to Mrs Mary Shaw, wile of Mr Thomas Shaw, Mlll-street,to tell how she had taken the girl Walker in to live with her, owing to the fact teat one night she had been locked oat by her grandmother, and how the girl had repre- sented all the articles were her own.—Superiatendent Pearson wanted ' to know, from this witnes., whether it was not a matter of fact, that she had not asked any queatious ci the girl's grandmother, until she thought she was hkely to get into difficalties over the affair ?—Witness replied evasively; but also admitted it was so. She had been away from home for a week, eaid if her daughters had worn the articles at all it was not to her knewledge.—Constable Carringten took up the story at this stage, and told how he had again traced the stolen articles, and arrested the girl. On Saturday morning he had asked Mrs. Shaw about the girl being there, and if there were any of the goods there. She replied " She would have a look," and later brought the costume down to the Police Station with the remark that she had found it in the empty house neat door amongst some straw. On chargieg the girl Welker with the offence, she admitted it, and said " I took them all, and took thorn all to Mrs. Shaw's. Polly had this on a week last Sunday. We had tea together and went to the Chapel in the evening. Martha Shaw bad this on some time er other, and I was wearing this on Sunday," aeu indicated different costumes.

_ Prisouer elected to be summarily dGalt with, and in reply to the bench, said it was ter compauions that brought her up to it. The Chairman (Mr. Jtmes Fiendloy) : You have hen in Chester fGr some time, would you like to go back? Prisoner : Yes, sir. The Chairman : Will you promiso to be a good girl if we Fend you there? Prisoner : Yes.
The Chairman : Very well. We will send you to Chester, nut if you are not a good girl, you wilt be brought here again and will be dealt with in, a way you will not like.
Prisouar was then bound over in 403 to come up for judgment when called upon.
-Tiie Cnairrn‘n then ;eprimanded the witness Shaw, and told her to be careful of anything of the kind in the Suture.
Witness : Yes sir. This will be a lesswa to me What I did I only did in kindness.

A Boy Robs a Ketch.'" William Bailey, a 11 year old boy from Worsley, was charged with two offences of larceny. The first war the theft of a pair of gloves, and a rug, value 7s, the proporty of A. Ryan Steohen, captain of the ketch 'Friendship"; and the second, the tneft of a coat and vest, 15.; pair of drawers. ss; j.-q+ey, 3s ; vest, 3s; jack's', 2+; pair of drawers, 2s ; and a cap, is ; a total value of 314; the property of Albert Cann, A. 8., on board the " Friendship," both of which off,nces were committed on the 16th of June. From the evidence, it appeared that on Thursday last week, the boy came alongside the " FrLeriship " and asked for a job. The captain engaged him. On the Saturday the captain left the vrssel and came asnore about 10 o'clock a, night, leaving the boy in charge. Upon returning. about 11 o'clock, he found the boy was not there. He retired to rest, but upon the seaman Cann returning, the cantain was awakened by him, and told that several of his things had•been stolen,and Cann's chest, which was in the forecastle, opened. The article% already mentioned were missed. Information was given to the police, aed as a result the b)y was arrested by Acting-Sergeant Samuel Gregory, at the house of Mr. Jahn Baker, Norley-street. The whole of the goods were recovered. In answer to the charge the prisoner replied that the goods were given him by Cann. Prisoner now pleaded guilty, and elected to be sum- marily dealt with. Tne Chairman addressing him eaici : You have done very wrong, but if you will promise now not to steal anything again, you will simply be bound over? The promise was elven, and the prisoner bound over for six months, i= 403.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

A VIOLENT WOMAN AT STOCKTON HEATIL—At the War- rington Occasional Court on Tuesday. before Mr. F. A. Frost, a young woman, named sate Stanley, was charged with having been drunk at Stockton H•nith on Monday.—She pleaded guilty.—P.C. Thomas said the prisoner was not only drunk but was creating a great disturbance, and be had to lock her up. She had been " carrying on " for hours.—Jstnes Monks gave c)r- rnborative evidence, and added that the language the prisoner used was "simply disgraceful."—Prisoner now stated that she was ill,and that she was on her way to a home at Chester when apprehended by the police.— Sergeant Bourne: You would not have thought so, sir, if you had seen ber in the cells. You would not have thought there was much the matter with her. For five hours she used most disgracsful Irnguage until she became sober.—She was fined 73 6 ccsts.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF MISS MAY PIERPOINT.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF MISS MAY PIERPOINT.

The pretty, rustic, village of Grappenh all was the scone of more than usual life and activity on Tues- day, on the occa,ion of the marriage of Miss Mary (May) Pierpoiat (oldest daughter of Councillor William Pierpoiat,J.P., C.C., of Marlfield,Latchford) and Mr. Frank Earl Griffiths (son ot Mr. Charles King Griffiths, of Broken Cross,Northwicb). A large number of invited guests and friends assembled in the tine old church of St. Wilfrid, Grappenball, to witness the ceremony and tie correspondingly large attendance of the general public was an evidence of the bride's popularity in the district and of their interest in the proceedings. Here and there bunting was displayed in honour of the event and the Swing Bridge at Latchford was unusually gay for the occasion. During the assembling of the guests, the organist, Mr. Asquith Wood, played Wely's offertoire iu G and also an offertoire by Salome. Shortly alter 1.30, the bride arrived at the church and the ceremony immediately commenced. As the bright sun glinted through the stained glass windows on the well-dressed company present, pleasing ensemble was presented, and the prevailing opinion that the wedding was one of the prettiest seen in the district, strengthened: Bride and bride- maids all looked ch,-aming in their pretty hats and dresses. The service was fully choral and com- menced with the singing of tha hymn" 0 Father all creating" to music composed by Sir Arthur Sullivan for the hymn written in honour of the Queen's Jubilee. The officiating clergymen were the Rev Richard Greenall rector of Grappenall, assisted by the Rev F, A. Screeton, vicar of Christ Church, Latchford.

The bride was given away by her father. She wore a beautitul dress of poult.e de solo with trans- parent yoke, and sleeves of Brussels lace appllqu6, the swathed bodice being caught up at the left side with oranae blossom, myrtle, and heather. She also wore a tulle veil with a coronet of orange blossom, and carried a shower bouquetof roses, stephanotis. and orange blossom, her ornaments being a string of pearls. The bridesmaids, the Misses Margaret and Bessie Pierpoint (sisters of the bride), and Miss Monett and Miss Cottrell, wore white china silk drekses with insertions of Valenciennes lace (neck and sleeves transparent) and long trained skirts with insertion and frills. Their hats were made of white crinoline straw trimmed with chiffon and red and pink roses. They carried charming bouquets of pink and red roses, and wore pearl and gold pen- dants, the gift of the bridegroom. Mr. Sidney Griffiths brother of the bridegroom acted as best man.

At the conclusion of the ceremony the party re- tired to the vestry where the register was signed, During the while, the organist played Bach's " My heart ever faith ftil," and as the newly-married couple left the church Mendelssohn's " Wedding March " was played. A reception was afterwards held at the house of the bride's parents, over a hundred guests being present. Mr Bellew), of Chester, supplied the wedding cake. Later in the afternoon Mr and Mrs Griffikhs left for London, en route for Dieppe, amid plentiful showers of rice and confetti, and with the carriage baring the conspicuous badge of the newly-wedded--a pair of slippers. The bride's travelling dress was of dark blue cloth, Eton coat with white silk yew-, and collar edged with Russian lace. Photographs Were taken on the lawn of the bride and bridegroom, the bridesmaids and the wedding guests. The equipages were supplied by Mr 11 F Greenough. The EM- /qiEss, a narrow-minded, ignorant, and bitter reac- tionary, has allowed the Boxers to become what they are, and she is responsible for the chaos which Prevails. She could have put down the drillings and meetings of the Boxers, if she had honestly tried to do so ; but she has never seemed to realise that the Powers were sure to intervene, and that their intervention might ultimately affect her position and that of the ignorant men who have been her ready agents in seeking to eject foreigners and seal up China from the outer world. Whether She is conscious at the present moment of the gravity of the crisis we do not know. She seems to have prevented the Yamen from giving any I:ePly to the requests and protests of the Powers 111 Pelan. Her answer appears to have been the encouragement of the Boxers, conveyed in that subtle way which Chinese politicians know Se Well how to adopt. Unless we are totally deceived as to what ,has been going on since the middle of last month, the Dowager EMPRESS Ilas been in league with the Boxers, and had never given a thought to her own safety until foreign tr°oPs were landed. Then she seems to have had Bhille disquieting suspicions, and to have played a raere daring part than ever, calling in regular troops not to put down the Boxers, not to cheek them in their destruction of property, but to 'flake a show of resisting any occupation of Pekin. ifelv far she will now go, and whether the C4inese troops will be hurled against the contingents of the Powers, when they arrive near enough to ?ekin to be attacked, we do not know. Taku forts have been seized by the Powers, and we await further news with anxiety. But of this we are sure, that if the Empress and her Ministers do ot act with courage in assisting the Powers, there be a change in the occupant of the Throne and a new Government will have to be speedily established.

Its desire is to impress on 'us public that some of the vessels which figure in rir fleet lists are r3ally out of date and more or n e cient. Its manifestoes, however, would give the observer the idea that our navy is unsafe, 11,C1 would deter the budding youth from the Marines, for the first thing that wale recruit wants is security for his life against tUean dangers. It is not the intention of the 41 aV Y League to make it more difficult to fill the 'ranks of the navy. Quite the contrary; but the Poster system of agitation lends itself, as we have to misapprehensions. Again, there has been a great outcry about the number of foreigners terving on our ships. That matter should be tuia_ ndled carefully,for its repetition is liable to give impression that the lower-class work on our ;IPs is done by the scum of other nations, and at an able-bodied seaman will have to suffer very Unpleasant companionship. div.head: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
div.p: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
A Provincial Letter.

That railway servants are only human we appear to have been told by every writer who felt himself called upon to apply a "moral "to the railway disaster at Slough on Saturday. The truth of the saying is as self-evident as the adage itself is hackneyed. It affords no sort of consolation to the relatives and friends of the five persons killed, or to the injured and mutilated who barely escaped with their lives; and ic will require a good deal of drumming into the ears of railway directors yet, be- fore toe latter see the desirableness of placing Lwo men in each signal box, where there is only one at present. Yet this is what is meant, and aimed at, by the constant repetition of the saying, on these occasions. It has been urged again and again that the additional security would be cheaply purchased by the payment of the wages of a second man, and that passengers would not mind a slight increase of fares even for the extra safety which the arrange- ment would be likely to ensure. It is very well to plead the obvioumess of it's being to the interest of the companies, as well as of the public, that every precaution against acci- dents should be taken, but experience reminds us that many of the existing and approved precau- tionary measures. were wrung from, rather than conceded by the different companies concerned. So that, if on the understanding that railway servants, signalmen especially, are" only human," and that two in the signal box would be better than one, some such arrangement is really held to be de-ir- able, the next thing is for the public to Continue "pegging away" until they get it. There were about half a dozen M.P.'s in the Slough train on Saturday, and that should count, but in the next disaster there may be an Archbishop, and then the suggestion would be remembered. Athough it comes from America, the following will appear to some readers almost too good to be true. Mr. C. M. Sheldon, of "In His Steps" fame, h s been giving a Liverpool minisier some interest- ing statsments on the temperance question. Inter alla he observes that in America public opinion has advanced so rapidly with regard to the importance of total abstin- ence, that in some of the States the taking of intoxicants involves social prejudice. If, he is re- ported to have said, he were a drinker, and his con- gregation became aware of it, he would no longer be able to retain his pastorate. It may be that, something unexplained hangs on the meaning to be attached to the words "a drinker." If not, and the praise is accepted literally,it can only be said, more is the pity, prehaps, that for the present there is not much prospect of the people of England attain- ing so high a standar I of excellence on the question as these particular Americans, although there are reasons for encouragement. For did not Dr. Temple say last week, that whether temperance reformers in England, stood on " moral or scientific grounds, they were satisfied with their position, and knew it was impregnable ?" That seems about as good as the Americans can offer, and should at least be ex- ceedingly stimulating to the party. After threats of a slump in the labour market during the previous month, there was in May a de- cided improvement, with plenty of employment in a majority of the industries. There have been fewer disputes than usual between employers and workmen during the past month, and wages gener- ally have risen. The industries in which employ- ment appears to have been most difficult to obtain are the printing trade, the boot and shoe trades.and the woollen and worsted trades. The principal in- creases of weekly wages ware in the mining and iron and steel industries.

Mr. Preston Thomas is very severe with some of the poor-law unions coming under his cognisance as one of the Local Government Board Inspectors. He says that, owing to laxity of administration, people who are not entitled thereto obtain relief, and others follow the example. This, he says has two injurious results. It discourages thrift and in- dependence, while it prevents the Guardians re- lieving the deserving cases in an adequate manner. Thus an aged couple who cannot work are allowed two shillings or 2s 6d a week, out of which it often happens that they have to pay rent. The In- spector suggests that it would be better to reduce numbers and increase amounts. It would no doubt be well for the poor if all the Inspectors were to support Mr. Thomas's views.

Since the House of Commons has a committee sitting at the present moment to consider the mis- deeds of the army contractor, it can scarcely be assumed that he has been having an altogether pleasant time of it this year. It should interest those places engaged in the making of boots, espe- cially, to learn that the present style of army boot has been tried and found wanting at Pretoria. Hence a departmental committee is being formed to investigate the matter, and strange to say, is to make a nice little trip to Spain in search of an im- proved army footgear. To the present time cheap- ness has been the main object, and boots made in India have been adopted because of a difference of a few pence in the price. There are no doubt those in our own hoot-making towns and communities. who, if the War Office could make up its mind as to what it wants, and be induced to send down samples so that 106E11 boot manufacturers should have an opportunity of inspecting them, would gladly nut in tenders, both to show what thay can do and to make a little profit at the same time. Anent the inquiry being officially conducted as to the cause or causes of the railway accident at Slough. The public may be reminded that although they have been told automatic couplings are not required, no fewer than 2,848 railway servants have during the past six years lost their lives in shunt- ing operations. We rightly think a good deal of the five lives lost on Saturday last, but hers we have another hard fact that requires much explain- ing away. This waste of life is going on, too, at an increasing rate of five hundred cases per annum, and is equal to three deaths in two days throughout the year ! Where there are peculiar circumstances in connection with the accidents Board of Trade inspectors investigate, as one If them is doing now in the Slough affair, hut the returns show that dur- ing the six years already mentioned only 446 fatal accidents of the kind alluded to were made the sub- jects of official inquiry, while 2402 were not exam- ined at all.

Revived interest in the question of agricultural depression has been caused by the publication re- cently of the agricultural returns for last year. Some erroneous conclusions appear to have been arrived at. and it is necessary to point out that what may be regarded as telling mere of the depres- sion than even variations in the wheat averege is the steady contraction of the entire area of cultiva- ted land. Every year since 1892 the area of technically cultivated land shows a certain reduc- tion. It is pointed out, however, that this is partly male up by a smaller average of bare fallow. The diminution of the cultivated area is in some measure accounted for by the steady in- crease of population. the regular expansion of cities, and the annual demand of land for buillings Darks, and pleasure grounds to meet modern needs. It must at the same time be noted in this connec- tion that agricultural land taken for such purposes never appears to be compensated for by the culti- vation of hitherto waste land in other parts of the country; 80 that the diminution of the land under cultivation appears to be absolute. It may have been noticed by the reader that, there was a slight increase in the acreage under small fruit and orchards.

Mr. 3. G. Jackson, High Chief Ranger, of the Ancient Order of Foresters. is earning and receiv- ing high enconiams for the manner in which he discharges the important duties devolving noon him. A few days since " The Sonthern Daily Mail "praised his patriotic and whole-hearted con- duct in suggesting that the reservists should be kept upon the books of the Order while fighting their country's battles, and now "The Recorder," a newspaper which pays particular attention to friendly society matters, alludes to the "character- istic outspokenness" with which it has been attack- ing the reprehnisihle practice of some courts in seceding from the Order, taking with them a little nest-egg in th-! shape of the savings which have accumulated through the efforts of past and more loyal mernbars, The latter authority agrees with the High Chief Ranger that seceding courts, like seced- ing individuals, should be required to leave their funds behind them.

Mr. F J Norman said they had sent out from Runcorn circuit a very large coutingent of ministers, and their friend Mr. Bisbrown had been deputed to write to these gentlemen asking them to be present that day. Mr. C W Hutchinson Newcastle-en-Tyne, The Revs. S F CJllier, of Manchostr, J D Brynford Jones (Pockling- ton), J W Simister (Becakenhana), Edward J Hope (Cheslyn Hay), H Lewis (Davenport), Thomas Arrow- smite (Batley), and J H Taylor (Market Rasen), all old scholars at Brunswick, wrote regretting tht various circumstances prevented them from attending tne meet- ing.

IMcKenzie conducting a week's revival services. He remembered the old class leader, John Bailey. He still retained a string affection for old Brunswick, for Mr Simister's class, and for the Mutual Improvement Class. The likes of tfasin were not to be found anywhere else in Methodism. He should ever retain the liveliest and best recollections of the Bible readings by Mr. Simister. Brunswick would never die so long as people were true to it. They wanted to reach the people's hearts, and when once they had dome that they need have no fear in regard to the future. (App!ause.) Mr. A. R. Norman said he was proud to be treasurer of Brunswick Sunday School. He had now held that po:Fition for some years. He believed his position to-day was entirely due to the early influences and impressions made upon his mind in Brunswick Sunday School. He beieoed those impressions were such that would always stick to him, and serve as a guide and protection throughout the whole of his life. Whenever he had been tempted in days gone by to leave the school and to sever his connection with the church, those early impressions had come vividly to his mind, and he had felt con- strained to stick to the church of his fathers, and be hoped the church of his succeeding geueratioo. (Applause). Mr. J. R. Frith said it was 37 years since he entered Bruns wick as a teacher. He was born a Methodist, and although he did not find amongst the people of Runcorn the Methodist body to which he belonged, still he found another Methodist body. They had been his friends aver since. He united himself to Brunswick, and there taught a class. At the request of their old friend Mr. Simpson, he took charge of Mill-brow, as one of the superintendents. He telt proud to-day that he had been ceanected with "old Brunswick." It was there that he met his wife, and he remembered that the lady who sat behind him on the platform (Mrs. Hutchinson) was in Mr. Simpson's class for some years. (At this coils the Rev. F. W. Macdonald, President arrived, and as he appeared on the platform he was accorded a most hearty welcome). Mr. Frith,contlnuing, referred to the proposal to alter Halton-road chapel and said when he took the matter up some years ago he was shown the cold shoulder, Now that Mr. Norman had taken it up he felt sure the thing would go for ward,and they would have good accommodation all round. (Ap- plause.)

div.head: An Unparalleled Celebration.
div.p: An Unparalleled Celebration.
The President of the Conference at
Runcorn.

Never, perhaps, in all its chequered career has Runcorn witnessed a religious demonstration such as that which the last week end brought under our notice, when the Wesleyan Methodist building in the town celebrated the centenary of what they so lovingly describe as the "Sunday school work of 'Dear Old Brunswick.'" Last week we gave an historical review of "Nonconformist History of Runcorn," as a fitting preface to the celebration. This week, we try to describe, though somewhat inadequately, all that took place in the short, brigtat,week-end just passed, and which will ever be a sweet recollection to all Nonconformists of an histronic opportunity well-used and magnifi- cently improved. Look a moment upon the objects the celebration has had in view ! They are laudable in the extreme, and well have they merited the success which has attended their promulgation : " To permanently commemorate the centenary of the Runcorn Circuit Wesleyan Sunday Schools." the Sunday School Committee and the Circuit offi- cials decided :—first to erect new Sunday schools with suitable class-rooms at Weston Point, and at Preston Brook; secondly, to modernise Halton-road Chapel so as to provide chapel, Sunday school, and class rooms (the scheme adopted having the unani- mous and enthusiastic approval of the Halton-road Chapel and Schools Authorities), and thirdly, to provide" Old Brunswick" with a modern heating apparatus, and additional class rooms. The esti- mated lost of these undertakings are estimated at £2,000. This is indeed a monumental figure of Runcorn Wesleyan Methodist self denial; and, when considering the question of ever reaching it, especially in face of the already severe drain upon the resources of the cause on behalf of the Million Guinea scheme, those at the helm must have been fearful at their own audacity. But, in face of the result of their efforts, it is clearly borne out that their estimate of their co-religionists' zeal and mag- nanimitl was well founded, They were not depen- dent upon "a broken reed," and a record of generosity and self-denial has been established by " Old Brunswick" and her children, which is unparalleled in the annals of any other religious cause in the town.

div.head: BLESSING ON THE WORK
div.p: A BLESSING ON THE WORK

How fittingly was the celebration commenced, when the" Old Brunswickers " and their offspring gathered on Friday night, within the precincts of the venerable chapel in Brunswick-street, in a united prayer meeting. There was impressively asked of God a blessing upon the celebration about to be commenced. What was about to be undertaken was entered upon with fear,and trembling and thankfulness ; and not in a spirit of self- glory or boastfulness, and those, who rising from their knees, went forth f,•orn that peaceful, quie7, gathering, homewards did so with a beautiful" Thank God " for the blessings of a century's well-wrought work. For who that saw the great procession of the Saturday fol- lowing, would not feel convinced that nothing but a century's well-wrought labour could have produced it. The year 1800 saw the strength of the Sunday School as the str..rigtla of an infant. A mere handful of scholars, about 20 in number ; but by Saturday last they had in- creased, grown, strengthened, and prospered and borne fruit more than a hundredfold. Over 2,500 souls took part in the demonstration and paraded the street in one united procession which took about 20 minutes to pass a given point. The sight was magnificent, and the im- pression left upon the mind of the beholder inspiring.

div.head: OLD BANNER
div.p: THE OLD BANNER

Heading the vast cortege was the 1837 banner. True its appearance was much the worse for wear, but it recalled many happy reminiscences, especially to those old scholars who Immediately followed it in open landaus. They included Messrs James Bowyer, Jos-ph Fox, Thomas Millinger, Robert Brown, William Stubbs, S Ward, Mrs Elizabeth Johnson, andiMrs Basnett,whos,s combined ages reached abcut 640 years. or an average of 80. They appreciated the torn worn bannor. which most of them had seen unfurled in the year 1837. The inscription upon it was" Runcorn Circuit Wcslevan Methodist Sunday Schools, 1800." Following these truly " Old Scholars of Brunswick" was the Widnes Subscrip- tion Brass Band, and members of the St, Paul's Church congregation. Then came the

NEW BANNER, which had that very afternoon been unveiled in the presence of a large gathering, in front of " Old Bruns- wick," by Mr. Josep'a Fox. When doing so Mr. Fox spoke of his long conn(ction with the place as one that had brought him great anti lasting comfort. When the ceremony was over Mr, T. Simister led off three hearty cheers. The banner was a really beautifully hand painted affair, with the Bible in the centre of a sun of glory, and bore the inscription :—" Brunswick Wesleyan Methodist Sunday School, Runcorn, established 1800."—Mill Brow Wesleyan Sunday School followed with its scholars and officials, and their banner announced that the year 1845 saw their foundation. They were headed by the Hatton Road Choir, instead of a brass band, and en route several beautiful hymns were sung. Camden Wesleyan Sanday school formed the next section. They were headed by Gossage's Prize Bind, Widnrs, and their beautiful banner announced to all the year 1862 was that of their establishment, and that "the banner over them was love." Nelson itreet Seheol (Camden's lusty off-spring) headed by their own fife and drum band took up the next section of the pro- cession.and their exceptionally beautiful banner,perhape the most interesting in the whole procession, told of their foundation in the year 1878, and bore the command " Feed my Limbs." Holy Trinity Wesleyan Sunday School, headed by the Preston Brook Band,with 'heir historic banner of 1824, preceded the Preston Brook Sunday School. The latter were provided with a banner possibly the twin brother of the Old Brunswick 'Trophy, which headed the whole procession, but it was better preserved, and datel se, hence not so noticeable. The Elalton and Preston Brook contingents had provided decorated arts and !tarries for the purpose of carrying their little ones and these added a pleasant diversity to the spectacle. The Weston Chapel Brass Band headed the Sunday school scholars from that village. Their record dated from 1832. Several appropriate texts such as "The Bible our guide," " Children obey your parents" and " God Woes our school," appeared prnmineely borne aloft amongst them. The band of the Weston Salt Union, indicated the fact that ti the Weston Point Wesleyan Schools were behind. The I date inscribed on the flag of this school was 1872. The little ones of both the latter places followed in other fancifully bedecked conveyances and formed a fitting conc'usion to a most imposing and inspiring pageant. After wending their way from Brunswick Schools via Church-street. Waterloo-road and Bridee, Shaw-etrret, Greenway-road, High-street, Bridge-street, Halton-road, and back to Fountain tocluare, the vast concourse of people massed in a compact gathering, and at the invitat'on of the Rev. C. W. L. Christien (the superintendent of the circuit), sang very impressively. " Praise ye the Lord," All Hail the Power of Jesn's name," and the " National Anthem." Subsequently they dispersed to their various billets for tea. The scholars on parade were :
