4)t snven o'clock a public meeting was held in St. Paul's Church. While the congrneatiin were ssAembling A number of popular hymns war,. sun, the Rev J A B Malvern acting as conductor. The chair was occupied by Mr T Simister (senior superintendent of Brunswick), and he was supported by the Revs CW L Christion (superintendent of the circuit), S Wright, Morrison, C E

div.head: INTERESTING LETTERS
div.p: INTERESTING LETTERS

Mr. Norman, coquetting, said they had not hewed from the Rev 11. Ravenscraft, who was in Africa, but his (Mr. Norman's) brother was there in person. There were two letters teat they could not pass by without some special reference. N 3 one had looked forward to that centenary with greater eagerness ana delignt than Mr. John Daniel Jones. (Applause.) They all knew how ill he was. Ho (Mr Norman) had written to him the other day, not about that centeaary, and he believed Mr Jones was propped up in bed to write a reply. His letter was couched ia the following terms ;—" It is an intense disappointment to me to be laid aside just at the time of the celebration of the ceatenary of'Dear old Brunswick.' to which I had looked forward with such eager anticipation. I hope you will be favoured with fine weather for the procesSion. and that my friend Mr. Povah will be equal to the demand that will be made on the commissariat department. I think he will, however. If I could have been at the meeting on Saturday night, and an opportunity had presented itself, I should have taken great pleasure in testifying that all I have that is worth possessing, and all that I am that is worth while, I owe, under the pro- vidence of God, to Brunswick Sunday School, and its great superintendent, Mr. John Simpson. I was so little when I was taken there as a scholar that I cannot recall the event. The names of four teachers stand out more prominently than the rest as influencing me—Mr Joseph Fox, Mr Charles H Kent, Mr John Ocaleston Jackson, and Mr William Eaton. I joined Mr. Eaton's society c ass in 1866, and I have been a member of society ever since. You know of the happy associations of the imprevement class, that wonderful monument to the faithful devotian and zeal of our dear friend Mr. Simister—a class it would be difficult to match in Methodism. I don't wish to write as if everythiag was coming to an end. The new century only begins a new era of conquest, an.] [every kopje taken matits a new frontier line to be defended, and from which fresh advances shall be made on the kingdom of evil. I firmly believe that the young strong hands in which the fortunes of the school are fast falling will prove equal to the task. God grant they may." He (Mr. Norman) was sure the congregation would heartily agree with the following telegram being despatched to Mr. Jones :—"Your old schools celebrating their c mtenary deplore your absence and pray God for your speedy re- covery." (Applause.) Mr. Simpson wrote as follows: —"titan Morfa, Conway, sth May, 1900.—Dear Mr. Norman.—l feel grateful to my Runcorn friends for their kind remembrance of me, and the wish that I should be present at the Sunday School Centenary Cele- bration, but I am so infirm and helpless, and my health is so uncertain, that lam sorry to say my coming is quite oat of the question. Besides this, my hearing has become so bad that lam not only shut out from all et:tine matters, but it is very difficult to make me hear anything that is said ta me. Brunswick Sunday school lies very near my heart. It is upwards of 62 years since I became a teacher there, and ten years later I was appointed a superintendent (it is 70 years since I be. rna3 a teaeher in the first school I was connected with), and it is pleasant to think of the many good people I have known in connection with the school, and the great numter of scholars I rem-ember, many of whom are now scattered about in various parts of the world. The names of many who took an active Part in connection with the school earlier in the century-will not he forgotten such as good old William Holt,Jonathan Potter, and William Dutton, and others, as Mr. Kent and Mr Soulby who passed away more recently. The Wesleyan Sunday Schools in Ruccorn have been a great blessing in tke past, and my earnest prayer is that they may be much more abundantly bossed in the future. It is very pleasant to be remembered, and again thanking nay friends for their kindness, believe me, yours sin• cerely, Joms SIMPSON% Fred J. Norman, Esq." They had decided to forward the following telegram to Mr. Simpson :—" Your old schools celebrating their centen- ary recognise your magnificent wotk in the past, and pray God to grant you a peaceful eventide." (Ap- plause.)

div.head: TESTIMONY OF OLD SCHOLARS.
div.p: TESTIMONY OF OLD SCHOLARS.

The Chairman expressed his gratefulness that he had been considered worthy to occupy that poition. He was taken to Sunday school when ho was five years of age, and he had been attending over since. For 18 years he had been at Sunday school at his home, and 13 years in Manchester. On October Ist, 1857, he came to reside in Runcorn, and attended the Brunswick Sun- day school the following morning. He had been going there since that period, and honed to go as long as he possibly could. He did not think that anyone could more truly say " Dear old Brunswick "than himself. It became more dear to him year by year. He could not possibly describe the associations of that institution. When he first joined the school he never thought he could settle in the church or in the school. In 1859 the Rev. Peter McKenzie visited the place—(applause)—and gave a turn and impetus to Methodism in Runcorn which had attended it all along from that day.Fle now felt that to leave Brunswick School would be a very great trial in deed. No one could conceive what evils be had beensaved from, and no one could descri'ne the blessings which had come to him by being associated with that church. He urged all the young people whatever they did to keep to their Sunday school and congregation, and to the wor- ship of God, and never allow anything to entice them away. If Sunday schools were to live they must be carefully attended week after week. That had been a grand day for him. They were beine• bound together from Preston Brook to Weston Point, and they were beginning to feel that they wanted every school in the circuit to prosper. (Loud applause.) Mr. F J Norman read the following telegram which had been received from the Rev John Walter Simister : —" Sorry not to be with you for auld tang svne ' Hearty congratulations, best wishes for successful cele- bration."

The Rev C W L Christien next addressed the meeting. He referred co the men who had gone from Brunswick into the Wesleyan ministry. They were good men and true. Some were working at the theatre of war, and they were doing good work which would spring up afterwards. From Brunswick School had gone forth streams of holy influence that bad blessed the world far and wide, and 01 necessity would bless the world still farther and wider in the future. They were not going to say die just yet. Judging from the demon- stration that day it looked as though Runcorn Sunday schools friends hal some dislike to dying. They thanked God for their position and for the holy power there was in Runcorn Methodism that thy. That anniversary had adopted a scheme for the benefit of the Sunday school work in the circuit. They were going to do four things. They were going to erect a mucb-needed new school at Weston Point ; another at Preston Breek ; new classrooms at Brunswick ; and a Sunday school at Haltoo-road. He hoped that they would be able to say when the meeting closed on Monday that they had got the £2,000. which was the estimated cost of the seheme. Applause.) Mr. Peter Lewten, an old scholar, in a brief address, remark d that he was one of a family of twelve. RA was the first to join Methodism, and it had been the grandest thing he ever did. For 21 years he had met in class, and the good he ha i received he had attribeted to " dear old Brunswick " His asociation W;th the pre- sent members ef the school was one of the blessings of his life. (Applause.) Mr Joseph Harrisen, another old member, and now statioemaster of Edgehill, said it was nearly 30 years since he crossed the bridge, and first put his foot in Runcorn. At that time he was only 13 years of age. and on to that period he did not know much about Methodist people. Had he heard ths name mentioned he should have treated it with contempt, because he had been brought up at the little Established Church i his native village in Lancashire. Mr. Harrison related how he lodged with a Mrs. Leadbetter whose influence attracted him te Brunswick Sunday School and was the means of him becoming a staunch abstainer. He was not ashamed of being a Methodist that day. He belonged to one of the best churches trs Methodism in Liverpool (he referred to Lorlee-lane),and he always told them that if they wante I t 3 know what a Sunday school annivereeey was they should came to old Brunswick. He hoped that GA's blessing might rest with them all. (Applause.) Mrs. Simkin, one of the lady scholars, who was warmly received, spoke a few appropriate words of gratitude to the teacher; who had been of such material assistance to her in Brunswick School.

The Rev. C. E. Norman said Brunswick School would always remain his school. He should never be able to mea.ure the full extent of his indebtedness to old Brunswick. It was 12 years since he left Bruns- wick school for D;dshury College, and he had a Bible in his possession with an inse,ription in its pages. At the hlttnm were the no.; es of Mr Simpson, Mr Sitniter. and Mr Edward Taylor. the young men and women of St. Paul's (tongregation could not have a grarrier home th to old Brunswick. It was connected with very many sacred memories, and it held a record that very few places could look back upon. There were too many mere worshippers in the church,and he hooed that the young men and young women would become workers. (Ap- plause.) Mr. A. Hughes said he had been trying to demide the pint "Why am I a Methodist ?" and he had failed. But there was onnthine he could tell them, and that was married a Mencdist sod had been happy ever since. It was something like 43 years since he went to Brunswick school, and he could remember Peter

div.head: ADDRESS BY THE PRESIDENT.
div.p: ADDRESS BY THE PRESIDENT.

The President of the Conference, who was cordially received, said he was much obliged to them for their vary genial and kindly welcome. It had been a year of unparalleled action and effort through- out their enti.re cennexion. He had indeed, been a travelling preacher during the past elevsn months. His j iurneys had varied between Penz wee in the south-west and Aberdeen in the nortie.and he seemed to have taken the places which lay between those ex- treme points. He began to fear that his children, and especially the younger portion of them, would gradually drift into the idea that their father was A myth', a faith, or a tradition—(laughter)-30 it was wel on behalf of those interests which were present for ever almost that he should from time to time keep, at all events, oa speaking acquaintance with the members of his family. (Laughter.) He was now on his way to attend the Co ference of the lish Methodist Church. There was very much that was joyful, and happy, and wholesome in the relations between the presidents of their Conference and the great body of brother minis- ters and the still larger body of their churches. It was a bad sign for any church,or any civil commun- ity, when its own principle offices were held in contempt, when the oceup ants were not sustained within their legitimate sphere of duty. He should think that English institutions were on the road to decay when there was a general disposition to disparage the men ho bore the principal offices, whet her in religious, civil, or political life. (Hear, hear.) He appreciated the loyalty of his brethren in the ministry and their people, north, south, east, and west. It would be a very large task to attempt to dive thorn an aceouat of his impression; of the life and conditio a of cneir churches. There had been, he should think, hardly equalled activity and generosity in local extension, and an amount of enterprise in school building, renovations, enlargements that he had very little doubt, when they came to be scheduled and tabu- lated, and they had all the statistical results before them, they would become amazed at the amount of money involved, and the religious activity and earnest- ness which those figures would suggest. He had bad the the pleasure of opening new chapels in villages and in towns, in little smiling agricul- tural et parishes, and in reugh coal and iron villages, among the miners of Cornwall and Durham. Their land was deserving of all their Christian work could do for it. The providence of God had been giving them all lessons in practical petriotis n, and he trusted that one of the compensations that woald survive the disasters, the sorrows, and 1033633 of war would he a deeper sense of national life, of national responsibility. of brotherhood to each other, to all classes and ranks of men in the c -immunity, and would stir in tens of thousands of British hearts the deep-seated feeling that they had a great responsibility of love towards God and their fellow men, and a desire that He would give them power, energy, and strength thet they might fuiel a noble trust. (Applause) To them it might not be given to shares the destinies of empires, hut they ceuld contribute to purify, strengthen, and inspire teat moral and spiritual life which, whether •it was found in the palace or in the cottage, was the real foundation and spring of their coun- try's happiness and prosperity. (Applause.) Now they were indulging in memories of the past. They were recalling the history of associations of their church in the town during the period that was past. But it could never be the main occupation of men and women to live with their faces turned upon the pest. (Heer, hear.) They must continually draw streteeth,inspiratioa and motive from the past, but it was to be applied in the present, and with a later(' view of the future. They had good reason to love their church with a love derived from the memories of what under the blessing, of God it had been able to do, for the names of their fathers, the records of their characters, their lives, the memories of what they did. These were all the rich annals of the past. They were utilizing this great memorial celehra, don, not merely to feed the mind with Woman': memories of the past, but to engage in large and gener ous enterprise for the future. They must all do their hest, and remember their responsibility. Than their Lord,the only true head and guide of His Chuece.would conduct their efforts te a happy and successful issue- (Applau,e.) Mr. Walter Millington also addressed the meeting. re- ferring to the beneficial influence coring men had derived Irons old Brunswick and its ins autions. A collection was taken in aid of the Circuit Scheme, and the meeting closed with the Benediction. During the evening several old favourite hymns were sung. THE PRESIDENT ON METHODISM AND THE CHURCH.

The services on Sunday were invested with mcrie than usual interest, because Peasideet Macdonald was t occupy the pulpit morning and evening. At both ser- vices the spacious edifice was taxed to tie uttermost to find accommodation for the large gathering of wor- shippers. A special and most enjoyable feature was the Ringing of old Methodist hymns, the favourites of a past generation, by the choir and scholars, who did credit to the training of Mr. John Birkett, Mr. G. Sawyer ably presiding at the organ. Amongst the items 'calling for special mention was the c lent " Oh the flowers of summer," the well-balanced choir disolayine power and sweetness of tone. The chants "Now the day is over" and "Jerusalem the Golden (sung by the desire of Mr. John Simpson) were other beautiful selections. The Presi- dent based his morning's sermon on Deuteronomy ii., 8, and in the course of an eloquent and scholarly discourse he said they were looking back, undoubtedly, upon one of the notable centuries in the land of their birth. Toe century which was closing had been one of extraordin- ary activity in nearly every province of human life. It was a remarkable century for the development and pro- gress in their national life. Tnere had been a wonderful ' religious quickening bf life and character in the history of the Christian Caurch of this country. Everywhere the community was nnurished.guided and blessed by the spiritual life and manifold labaurs which were suggested to men by Methodism. Religious progress had not been merely confined within church walls. Methodism had been involved in all the pro- gress of the centary. It had shared in the advance, the expansion, the uplifting, the moral and philanthropic progrets for which it was conspicuous. He c'aimed that the movement known as Methodism made an altogether unique tribute to the moral life, and, censequently, to the social welfare of this coultry. And through this cluntry it sent out the same influence over those wider areas to which the Eeglish- ;peaking peeple had moved. Sometimes they were asked was it not a ryty that Methodism had not, returned to the Chnreh or England. He was unwilling to speak on this subject at all. The question carried with it an import ant misun- derstanding, that Methodism never separated from the Church of England. This was a paradox he ,wou'd ask them to weigh. It never scparated from thc Church of England because it never belonged to it. thi, Ciourc'a of England never appointed one Methodist preacher, local preacher, class or lesder,er quarterly meeting. It ncvir governed, guided, subsidized MEthodisin in ary torim There never was any pniod of secession. Methedign took with it no building, no endowment, nothing that belonged to the Church. Somelmes they. were asked were they sure, that their orders to sacraments were v did ?Afeire again he was un- willing to dilate upon iteiletabi when he was told that, as he had been occasionally, that his order was not valid. and that their sacraments Were illegitimate, he was compelled to say that this *ea a question which was either the simplest in the world and the meat easily dealt with, for it was 038 of the most diffieelt and abstruse. If the Gospel of Christ was preachF d for the I guidance of human souls, and if spiritual life was up. held by that work and noerished then the validity of the case or genuineness was one which was immedi- ately s.ttlel. If on the other hand, they examined ecclesiastical literature, by which the validity of the orders was decided, he admitted that the difficulties were great. But they were no greater for them than for others. Within the last three years a very careful i,,n- quiry had been made by an infallible and august ecclesi- astical authority in Chris'endom as tolthe validity of the orders of the Church of England. The inquiry lasted , several months, and experts were engaged, and the 1 result was a formal authoritative statement that the

orders and sacraments of the Church of England were invalid, that she had no true ministers, no true sacra- ments. He told them candidly that he did not for' a moment believe this, and be was sure their Anglican friends did not believe it. A devout,pious clergyman in the Church of England—a man full of excessive veneration for the Roman Courch—wben he was told that the Church's sacraments and orders were invalid, said "it is vain to tell me that the spiritual organisatian which brought me in the Church of Carist was illegitimate and illegal.' The good man was right. He cut his way through the threads of laboured sophism, and knew better, for he had received spiritual life and important blessings in the Church which was called invalid. It was as essen- tial to-day as ever it was that the soul should b 3 in per- sonal union with Jesus Christ. Faith in Chris c as the Redeemer was as necessary to salvation as it was in the darkest days. In the evening the rev, gentleman preached from Luke iv. 19. MONDAY'S MEETING. ADD HESS TO YOUNG PEOPLE.

On Monday evening a public meeting was held in St. Paul's Chapel. There was a large attendance. Mr S Taylor presided, and he was supported on the platform by the Revs F W Macdonald, T d Bailey, G B Saul, C L Christian, El Morrison, C E Norman, J A B Malvern, T S Morris, H Barraclough ; Messrs Simister, F J Nor- man, Alt Norman, R H Posnett, Jams Handley, Dar- risen (Liverpool), I' A Pritchard, J R Frith, James M Frith. James Boote El Rawlinson, S Pope, Alfred Harri- son, E Taylor, G Bellamy, W Millington, &e. The Chairman, who was cordially received, explained that he had just come from ScAland, and said he pre- sumed he had been asked to oceupy that position as an old scholar of the Brunswick School. (Hear, hear.) It was something like 55 years since he first went to the old Brunswick Sctooel—(hear,hear.)—whea he was be tsveen five and six years old, and he could rem:envier many happy circumstances and many p' eoele who took an active and leading part in the school at the time. Tee late Mr. William Dutton was the superintendent— (applause)—and he also remembered a number of old friends who had passed away not very lens: ago. He saw one present that night—(Mr. J. Fox)—who was a teacher in his time. (applause.) Tlaire were also two others whom he remembered perfectly well as teachers, and to whose classes he belonged at various times. They were Mr. John Baden and Mr. Crawford. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He was in the latter'a class for some time. Then as time went on their old friend Mr. T Simister came to tee towa—(applause)—and he formed a select class. He wen; to that class for some veer-seam] remembered so well that the class consisted of young men from 15 to 16 up to old men over 50 years of age, and he wished to pay a tribute to Mr. Simister for what he did at that time and what he had done since. (applause )..11I; conclusion he strongly appealed for support for t school extensions scheme. The Rev. F. W. Macdonald met with an enthusiastic receplion, the whole audience rising en masse. In the course of his prefatory remarks the President said it had been very pleasant for him to take part in that most ehee:ful encouraging, and heart-stirring commemora- tion. He found at once that there was a great amouat of vitality, geed feeling, kindly co-operatioc, and earnest hopes and plans for the future inspiring that great movement. He was greatly impressed on the previous day as he looked upon the congregation that was just able to gather within those spacious walls, and the feature of that congregation that touched him most deeply was the large element of young people present. (Hear. hear.) He had clung to his own youth as long as he could with any decency, and nevertheless his sympathies, hie goodwill, his best wishes and his most sacred hopes wore bound up with the lives of their young people. If the noble brigade of men and boys, and they woald forgive him when he said ,he still more attractive brigade of young worn 'n and girls, would make the best of the opportunities and advant- ages they possessed, if they would endeavour to fulfil the hopes of those who loved them best, and would respond to the call and guidance of God, happy useful lives lay before them. He rejoiced to cherish the hope that they had there in larao numbers the citizanship of the next generation receiving the impress of Christian truth and principle, having its sympatWes and aspir- ations directed towards the Wit and worthiest objects. as one who, like the Chairman, had traversed the years by which youths advanced train youth to middle age, he shauld like to add his friendly and kindliest exaertation that they would, in those early years, begin well, hold to the good, make a true start in the spiritual, moral, and mental life,and take care of the advautages that were to came to lead them on from strength to strength. He was greatly delighted on the previous day with the singing of their youneer friends, let him say that of them. (Applause.) He was quite persuaded that under the modern conditions or church life it was a positively suicidal p licy to allow the services of praise in their places of puolic worship to be dull, spiritless, stagnant, uninviting, or even as he had known it from time to time, repellant. Is was hard enough under the dissi- pating infi lances that abounded to bring the masses of the;r p ipulatioe to the house of G 1, but they must not add to their diffieulty that of spiritless and wearisome se:ahem of song. Without 13:dag pedantic or too el abor , ate, he should say that two events had taken place in the history of their country, without which it was im- pessiblo that they should have assembled there taat evening, and for toe purpose that now fi led their minds The first of these causes was the reformation of religion tares centuries ago.—(hear. hear)—and the second was,- the revival of religion a century and a half ago. (Hear, hear),lt was quite obvious that had there beet:an reforma tion the vary ideas and principles that were represented there would not have had much chanee. They were not only the outcome of the reformation but they were chil- dren of the revival of religion. The rev. gentleman went on to refer t 3 the character of John Wesley—a maa. he said, who was the foremost agent in this great work. There never'was a ruin who had the unmistaks- able qualities of leadership more prominently than John Wesley. (Rear, hear.) He came of a good stock. He had no vicious youth from which to shake h'm self free. He grew up its an Enelisa parsenage. He had the b.st education that England of its day could afford. But for what parpese did Wesley use his gifts? To make money ? He said towards the end of his life " If I leave £5O behind me call me a dishonest man." He left shout 911 and two silver tea seoens. There was no an office open to a diviae that We,ley coald not have had, if that had been his object. He held his great powers ever as in the great Task-master's eve for Christ tad Ui Kingdom, and he used them to raise the fallen, to save the lost, to recover the brutal and godless multitudes to religion and morality, to carry the inspiring and consol- ing powers of Christianity deeper and deeper into the heart of the English nation, and from the English nation out over the widening surface of the wail Ito the far horizon of the West and of the South. (Anplause) At the present moment the impress of John Wesley's persenality, the results of his works were even to be found lying on the serf ace in ths religious faito,the tone and type of religious character, the very phraseology and balance and proportion of theological and religious thought in Great Britain, United States of America, the vast dominions of Canada, and the. Aastralsian Conti- nent, in South, Western, and Central Africa, and indeed here and there in every extending centre of light in the whole heathen population of the East. He did not say it was hard te speculate as to the future of the Church,' as to the redistribution of the lan is and the possessions of the earth, and the new forms of political life and social organization would take in the coming century. They might learn this at the Motile! Improvement Class, but meanwhile they must take the higher and still nobler thought that it was for them to be a servant of this world's Redeemer, for them to be a disch3h3 and witnes and worker for Jesus Christ. (Laud applause.) The Rev.G. B. Saul, superintendent of the Widnes Wesleran Circuit, also delivered a short address. Mr J. R. Frith said he knew they were all anxious to know what the CD lections were, and they would b- de- lighted t o learn that through that centenary celebration, although they could not give them the precise arneent that night, they saw their way clear to go on with the who'e of the scheme at once and they were assured that the £2,000 w arid be realize'. (Applaus There was one gentleman to whom they were very much indebted for all that he had done in connection with that effort. But far him that scheme would never have been formu- lated, the fund would never have been raised, ane the Sunday schools of the Rencern circuit would have gene nn marking time for a long while. He referred to Mr Free Norman. (Lehi applause.) Mr Norman had werked like a hero, and he (Mr Frith) was proud to think that the scheme would be a grand success. H. had groat pleasure in proposing that the best thanks of that meeting he given to their friend Mr Nerm an for his gigantic exertions on that occasion. (Applause.) The Rev. C. W. L. div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

A MAN CRUSHED AT WIDNES. On Saturday, a man named William Melton, 40, Charlotte-street, Whines, was admitted to the Acci- dent Hospital, suffering from injuries received by being crushed between two waggons and and an iron pillar. He was attended by Dr. Hutchinson. ACCIDENT TO A RUNCORN WATERMA.N. On Monday, George Smith, a waterman, residing in Hartley-street, Runcorn' met with a serious acci- dent at tee Old Quay Lock, on the Snip Canal, Run- corn. Smith was making a line fast to the canal wail, when tile rope became entwined round his leg. Tne unfortunate man's limb was terribly mangled. and she joint smashed at the ankle. fle was con- veyed by train to the Liverpool Infirmary. and ,successfully operated wean. DROWNING FATALITY AT WESTON POINT. , At the Weaver lintel, Weston Point, on Tours- 'day night, Mr. R Dobson, coroner, held an inquest upon the body of Donald Pater Burrows Bain, the four year old son of Mr. Donald Beim, joiner, whose ' body was recovered from the Weaver Canal the previous night. —Another little boy Henry Hughes, ' deposed tnas both 'went to Post Office-lane, from, whence the deceasen got on to the canal bank.—No evidence was forthcoming as to how the boy got into the water, and the jury returned a verdict of "found drowned." Mr. Kodick, the foreman, asked. the coroner whether it would not be advisable to recemmend the fencing off of the Canal ?—The Coroner replied that as the place was private pro- perty it would be useless making any representa- tion.—The Police were represented by Superinten- dent Gill, and Constable Carrington. THE STRIKE AT RUNCORN DOCKS. There is no change to report in the attitude of either tile Ship Canal Company or the boat loaders who are on strike. The masters appear as deter- mined in their refusal as the men are determined in their demand. In the meantime there is no clay being loaded at Runcorn for the potteries, and a number of boats have returned to the works light. A coneiderable quantity of clay has been loaded at Weston Point, and the manufacturers have not up to the present had much difficulty in keeping up their supplies of raw material. When that time comes, probably there will be a new development for the present deadlock would spell riLination. In some quarters a fear has been expressed that the traffic would be diverted to Weston Point, but in well informed quarters this possibility is deemed very remote, as the Weston Point Docks have not the requisite accommodation which could only be provided at an expense whicia the Weaver Trustees would be very unlikely to incur. THE LOCAL VOLIINTEERS. On Friday General Sherringeam inspected the Cheshire, Manchester, and London Rifle brigades on Salisbury Plain, and was highly pleased with the result. He was pleeoed to note the improve- ment in the discipline and control of fire and the steediness and intelligence of the non-commissioned officers and men when at manoeuvres, and considers that great credit is due to the officers for the man- ner in which they appear to have iraperEed instrue- T ion. The discipline and conduct of all ranks has been exemplary, and he has no hesitation in saying that he would be proud to take such a fine brigade upon active service. General herringham also )1c the opportunity of personally thanking the officers and men for their devotion to work during the fortnight's encampment. —Oa Sunday the great- est portion of the Runcorn companies of the 2nd Earl Cheshire Volunteer Battalion returned via Willies, and were accorded a hearty reception upon entering Runcorn, their march from the Bridgefoot to the Drill Hall being witnessed by thousands of inhabitants.—All ranks speak well of the excellent time they had under canvas. THEF.O OF NEWSPAPERS AT RUNCORN. At the Runcorn Police Court on Wednesday morn- ing, before Messrs. J. Ockleston (presiding), and W Handley, Stanley Rowles, 11 years of age, was charged in custody with stealing 20 newspapars, valued 101., the property of jabez Horracks, on the 11th of June at Runcorn.—Amelia Horrocks stated that she was the wife of Jabez aforrocks,newsagent, and resided in High-street, Runcorn. A bundle of 20 papers of the noon edition of the " Manchester Chronicle " was sent to her daily frena Manchester. On Monday,trie 11th inst, she sent one of the boys up to the railway station for the papers, but he returned and informed her that they had been taken away by someene.—Tnomeo.,Bowyer, school attend- ance officer, stated that he resided at Greenway- road, Runcorn. Oa Monday, the 11th June, he saw the prisoner with a bundle of newspapers under his arm. He gave chase after him, but could not catch him. Sergeant S. Gregory said he apprehended the prisoner at Bt3o a.m. that (Wednesday) morning. lie charged him with steal- ing 20 newspapers from the Railway Station on the 11th of June 1900. He replied "1 took them and sold some. The others I threw away," The boy elected to be summarily dealt With.—la answer to Ithe Bench he said iiis brother Percy and another lad had put him up to the theft. lie had been afraid to go home for fear of getting a hiding The previous night he had spent in a cellar.—The Bench decided to send the boy for four years to Bradwell Industrial Sceool,Sandbach,where he would be kept out of mischief and be taught a good trade. A DISPUTE OVER PLANTS AT WIDNES. At the Widnes County Coart on Friday. before his Hononr Judge Collier, Joen Hackney, Penketh, claimed a las for fixtures and stock-in-trade of a grocer's shop, 27, Alford-street, Widnes, less .£3 2s 61 for plants and flowers received from the de- fendant,lienry George Seddon, Alforde-street, leases ing a balance of ..-e5 7e 63. The defendant counter- claime „Ell 94 lid for plants and flowers sold to plaintiff Mr C Poole appeared for the plaintiff,and Mr J W Kaowles represented defendant. Mr Knowles admitted the claim of £8 103 and the claim for the plants was dealt with. The defendant spoke to Mrs Hackney agreeing to take over the plants and pay for them. James Halliday and. James Howson bath gave evidence that the plants were of good cpality and worth the value put On them by the defeleant. They were in good condi- tion. For the defence Mr Poole eorrended that when the defendant first mentioned about the dis- posal of the plants nothing was said about the price, and Mrs Hackney, quite expected that they were to be a gift. Mrs qackney,wife of the defendant Joseph S. ilvester and Joneeti in L xwrinzlon,gardeners ofil4re evidence. The two lest namel said the flowers and plants were not worth the price the de- fendant had charged. They valuel them at 413 and £4 10s respec.evely. His Honour thought that an enormously exaggerated claim, lie would allow the claim for the plaintiff, and £5 for the defend- ant. As credit amounting to £3 23 6 1 lied been given, the amount for the defendant would be £1 17s 61. Costs would be granted to each.

A FEROCIOUS DOG IN AIRIN-STRRET—BOYS BITTEN. On Monday at the Warzington Police Court, Joseph Bate, 30. Aikin-street, was summoned fer ha,ing on the 12th of June allowed to be at large unmuzzled in Aikin- street, a ferocious dog.—A little by named John Nox stated that last "I uesday afternoon at 530 ho,,was play- ing in Aikin-3treet when defendants collie dog flew at him and bit him on the leg. Ho had to go ro the Infir- mary to have the wound dreesed.—Walter Yatee,another boy, stated that he was hitt:Az by the dog three or four month a kince His mother complained to Mrs. Bate and she said she "wished the deg would bite another boy who kept going into the yard." Lionel Muir said that he was going to school last 7fuesday.He was crogsing some waste land behind Akin-st-eet when defendant's dog bit him on the leg. He had to go to the Infirmary and have the wound cauterized.—Frank Muir stated that two months ago the dog bit him on the neat. He was under treat- ment at the Infirmary fora fortnight. His mother com- plained to Mrs. Bate, and she s,.id it was not her fault. —Mrs. Muir said that the dog flew at her.—Wiliam Bar- low said he was bitten on the arm by the dog 18 month:, ago.—Defendant said that boys annoyed the dog by throwing stones at it. He had had the animal destroyed. —The Beech conuidezed ic a very serious matter, and imposed a fine of 25s including costs.

It was one of the worst cases of rowdy ism.he thought, that had ever bees before the Bench. It was certainly the worst case that bed been brought to Court since he had b!en Chief Constable and he asked the magistrates, if they convicted defend- ant to inflict a substantial pensity.—Berjamin Burdett, a driver for the Great Central Railway, who r-i•ides at 40, Ashton-street said that at 10 o'clock on the night in questi( n ho and his wife were gin one of Mr. Connor's 'bases comine from Fearnffead. Warrington Borough Court. FRlDAY—Before the Mayor (in the chair). Councillor Smethurst and Mr. J Hepherd. (the money forma in his possession) for being drunk and disorderly in Butter- market Street at 8.30 on Thursday evening. AN IMPeoveafeetT.—The adjourned case in which Joseph Towers and Martha Ellen Towers of 17 Ernest Street were charged with neglecting their children came up for hearing. —Mr. Browne, who appeared on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C. stited that since the seijournrnent there had been an improvement, and the case was withdrawn. , ASSAULT ox A NV o..teer.—William Oakes was charged I with assaulting Betsy Birchall, River-road, on June 9th Mr. Browne prosecuted and defendant was represented by Mr. Jenkins.— Mr. Browne stated that defendant came home at seven o'clock in the evening under the influ nce of drink. He put his basket down in the yard and exclaiming" Now for a :ow" rushed at Mrs. Birchall, who was the next door neighbour, struck her in the breast and twisted her wrisP. A daughter came to her assistance and defendant threatened to break every window in the house —Mr Jenkins said the cause of the occurrence was a dispute between defendant'a wife and Mrs. Birchall. Defendant did not, however, intend to assault her. —Defendant was bound over and ordered to pay the costs. Chrimes.—The officer stated that he found the prisoner lying down on the footpath drunk and asleep and partly undressed. Ile aroused him and he commenced to use very bad language. He asked him to go home And be refused, and kicked witness three or four times on the leg.— The Chief Constable; That was for awakening him up from his stony bel.—Witness, continuing, stated that with tha assistance of PC. Turne, he took prisoner to the Police btation He was very violent on the way.—Pined 10a and costs A ;4 ILITtaIfAN IN TROUBLE —Thomas B ,guley, a militia- man, and William Patten were summoned for committi 1g a breach of the peace by fighting in Queen-street on June 13th.—Patten did not appear and the Chief Constable said that during the course of the fight the man slipped and broke his ankle. He was taken to the Infirmary, awl it would be some considerable time before he eoald appear at court Basiuley stated that Patten struck, him first. lie (Bagule ) had just returned from the front.—He was bound over to keep the peace and ordered to pay 2s 6d costs.—The case Hgainst Patten was adjourned sine die.

OVER THE BARRAERS WALL.—Daniel Pyne, of no settled abode, wet charged with having been found in Orford Bnrraelcs, with intent to commit a lelon7,at 1 15 on Mond ty night.—He said he went to the Barracks to join the militia —Provost-Sergeant Brandley said at the time stated he found the prisoner going towards the receiving room from the direction of the wall. He questioned him and he said he hal come througk the gate to join the militia. That was untrue because the sentries would not have allowed him to case. Eventually he admitted having climbed over be wall and WAS going to the receiving room for a night's lodging. He detained him. The roam was kept op.ln throughout the night because of the men coetinually going in and out. A quantity of clothing, &1., was kept in the ro.im. fwd. lately 'they had suffered greatly from pilfering by outsiden.— Priaener. was nit eligible for the militia on a^count of his age.— Prisoner was committed to gaol for a month.

MARGA:RTNE FOR Burre:R.—David end Thomas Watkins, grocers, Runcorn, were summoned at the instance of Mr. A Timmins. Inspector under the Food and Drugs Act, of Cise,eter, for that they on t .e 15th of May last, at Weston. unlawfully did sell to the purchaser an article for butter which was not of the nature and substance of butter.-11r. '3'homas Watkins, who appeared on behalf of the firm pleaded guilty.—Leonard Johnson, a young led, of 6, Hartley-street. said on the 15th of May, he went to Westoa Point, and pur- chased from Thomas and David Watkins. grocers, one pouud of butter for 10d. He asked whether it was margarine ? and the person who served him said it was not margarine When he came out of the shop he handed the article he re- eel rd to Mr A Timmins. who had sent him to musks, the purchase.—Mr A Timmins. the inspector, sail when he received the parcel from the last witness, ha entered the shoo and spoke to theeassistant telling him that Johnsoe had just purchased a pound of batter for him. The assistant replied that was so The Inspector then nee' him who be was and time he would divide the sample in the usual way, leaving him one portion ; taking another to the public analyst Dr Carter Bell ; and the third he now produced for tee court.—As the result of the analysis Dr. Carter Bell had issued a certificate to the effect that '' It eves net a sample of butter, but contained 100 per cent. of mergarine." Under the Margarine Act the article should have been enclosed in a paper with the word 'S elargarine " upon it in inch letters. He produced the paper in which the article was wrappeA to show it was not to marked.—The defeneant said there had been no intention to defraud. People asked for' butter" when they wanted "margarine" and even quoted as low as 61 and 4d a pound. The boy had supplied it passibly, on that uneerstand ng. There were papers and labels in the shop for the " rnarge-ine."—The Magistrates' Clerk : That %yid not do. You have been pro- ceeded against under the Food and Dregs ect ; they say you have sold them ATI article they have not asked for.—De- fendant : We will not sell" margarine " for butter in any case —The Char' man : You have done so in this instance.— Fined 40s and Li 33 4d costs- —Tho Chairman expressedthe hope that it would be a warning to the defendants to have proper people behind the counter. div.head: RELIGIOUS LIBERTY AT BURIALS.
div.p: RELIGIOUS LIBERTY AT BURIALS.

Is it a Question of Religious Liberty or Common Courtesy ? The Rev. F. E. Powell. Deer Sir,—Thanks for your expression of regret, had you been content with that you would have done wisely, but to attempt to shield your discourtesy under the plea of religious liberty is unworthy of yourself, for no one knows better than yourself that this is not a question of the principle of religious liberty, but simply a question of common courtesy. It is a question of a Christian minister takaag a mean advantage of a favour granted, to parade his own peculiar ritualistic practices en other people's pro- perty. Was it kind, expedient, good taste, or courtesy for you to do this tciing in our graveyard even though you could claim the right to do it?—which you know you cannot. Since I have had charge of the graveyard at Hill elicit), I have willingly permitted ministers of all sections of the Christian Church to officiate, when re quested—Roman Catholics, Unitarian, tee Eitablished Church, and the various Free Churches, and I know of none of them, who have abused the privilege, but yourself, and I ought to have received treatment as courteous from you, as from anyone else. Pins Romish priest did not even put on his official robes but appeared in his ordinary clerical attire—ma he carried no cross. It is true he sprinkled holy water on the grave ; to that I took no exception, as the ground was dry and water is always useful, in fact the priest of Rome from an innate sense of discretion and honoundid as little of the objectionable as possible, reducing it te a minimum—Commend me always to the genuine Roman- ist.—But you sir, were not satisfied with the ordinary service of the Church of England, with which your fellow clergy have for many years been perfectly !satisfied and to which we took no exceptioc, but must introduce an innovation which your own sense of the order of things ought to have made you feel would be offensive , to Baptists. Knowing you by reputation as an aggressive ritualist you must pardon me for believing this to be a part of your ritualistic propaganda. You officiated on the first occasion and discovered you had such liberty, thee you determined, on a future occasion, you would carry the symbol of your distinctive views iato the benighted (?) region of this Baptist territory ; the opportunity came and you said to yourself, now's the opportunity for test- ting these Baptists, and you did so in the manner des- cribed, without regard to their feelings, prejudices and principles, and even in direct violation ot the spirit and letter of the Burials Law Amendment Act of 1830. A sectioo of that Act you have quoted, but a little further on, you will find the following section, to which I call your attention "Any person who shall deliver any address, not being part or incidental to any religious service permitted by the Act, or who wilfully endeavours to bring into con- tempt or obloquy, the Ceristian religion or the belief or worship of any Church or denomination of Christians or any minister ot any ouch Church or denomination, will be guilty of a misdemeanour." Again we have this instruction in the Act : N.B.—" It is most desirable that those who are respon- sible for the conduct of funerals, should carefully avoid not only the cemmission of any legal offence, but any proceedings which may afford Just ground for com- plaint." I hold .that in the light of these sections you have been guilty of a "misdemeanour," for rightly or wrongly sve believe that the use of a brazen cross or other crosses at a religieus service to be contrary to scripture, the teaching of our Lord, the practice of the e qtly apostolic church and our own belief, and the use of it in our graveyard was an act of contempt upon our faith and practice.and WC) have therefore in your action a just cause of complaint. You have violated both the letter and the spirit of the Act of 1880. If you plead ignorance of our faith and practice I can only answer I am net responsible for your ignorance. In 'seeking my protest against your ritualistic observances on the occasion in question, lam only asking you to recognize the same spirit of conce•sion, courtesy, and Christian respect which the law demands of me if I officiated in your graveyard. But I am not responsible to the Act of 1880 but to an old trust-deed. Nevertheless I held we are far more tolerant and cosforni more Wily to the spirit of that Act, than is usually done in connection with Parish graveyards. All we do is voluntary, we demand no written notice, o, time limit, nor do we confine the nrivilege to ministers living in the parish, in these mat- ters we are broader and more catholic. I have refused 'no one, not even yourFelf ; protest is not prohibition. Compare ion. attitude with the many shameful evasions of the Act which come to our ear again and agate. Your conclusion therefore, that in consequence of my solemn pretest "some Nonconformists only mean by ?Thom liberty to prohibit and truculently to denounce all relioioaa beliefs and practices which do not accord with their own "is as ungenerous as it is unjust. In reference to the first case the main features of which you do not deny, you make this strange state- ment : "I did not officiate in your place of worship on precisely the same ground that Nonconformists when making use of our churchyards do not officiate in our places of worship." But sir ! We are not allowed to use your church on such occasions, and you are allowed to use ours. Where then is your reason ?' In respect to toe use of the objectionable cross, before I made my nrotest (not at the graveside,—as your letter implies), but in writing, I made sure that you did not use it always at funerals, and that you had not used it in our graveyard before, and I took the quiet, inoffensive method of writ lag you about it. 4fter the very first occasion on which ellen a thing had been done at Hill Cliffe. In this matter you are in conflict with your own church, and the use of the symbolical Cross is with you, simply a part, of your ritualistic propagenda and as such I am justified in protesting against its use, in our graveyard. You may take it any here else you like and can, but you have no right to bring it to our gravenard, than you have into our chapel or my house. Noth withstanding your sarcasm shout stone and flower crosses I can assure you it is seeing our consciences' belief and judgment, to use crosses of any kind at a religions service and if you cannot distinguish the essential difference between e brazen cross officially used at a funeral service and these other Crosses, then it i 3 useless for me to attempt to do so, but it is fairly clear to other people. I would remind eon that there can be no comparison between the rights conferred by law, upon Nonconformists to officiate in a parish graveyard,which is national property and can be claimed ny any in the parish, and the rights which belong to a private graveyard. You cannot expect the same liberty, but we have granted more, and yet you are not satisfied, unless freedom means license to set our faith and practice at defiance. Was there a more preposterous !and presumptive claim ever made in the name of religious liberty? Tolerance and religions liberty do not mean that either you or I hove the right to enter any private property or house, to declare our own distinctive views or thrust upon others practices which may be offensive. Such conduct is an outrage committed in tbe sacred name of religious liberty. To me it is a most astonishing thing and a neinful revelation that a minister of Jesus Christ,should in these enlightened days, attach so much importance to a Kindergarten systsna of religion and think for a morneut that the 'cross' which was foolishness to the Gr,chs and a stumbling block to the Jews was a wooden, brawn or other symbolical cross. Alas alas ! when Christian teachers can so pervert the truth I My first letter was never intended for publication,but was written as a protest against what I considered was a breach of ordinary courtesy, that unwritten law which Christians should observe more fully than others. I wrote strongly, for I felt strongly my faith had been outraged in cur own graveyard. Yet, I think, the mattir could have been settled between us, had you not msnitested an indecent haste in resorting to the public press, sending my letter to the press, without first asking my couse,t, or giving me an intimation, having your own reply in print on Thins lay, whilst I did not receive it until Friday. Pardon me sir, if I feel that in this matter also you have been discourteous—and I feel it will be time enough for me to submit any notice You suEgest, to the college with which I am connected wisen you have thoroughly mastered the elements of Christian courtesy and have learnt at least, to respect the principles of thorn in whose house you are as a guest. Now that you have full liberty to publish the corres- pondence, I hope you will be perfectly satisfied—as for me Ido not fear the verdict—but whether the public think with me or not,l hate your ritualism,and while you can march and geneflx and carry as many symbols as you like and to your hearts content on your own ground, thank God there is still sufficient tolerance and liberty in England, not to compel me to have your crosses, incense and other nonsense, is' my own house, or in connection with my own church.—Yours &co JAMES SAMUEL HUGEIE3.
Stockton 11.ath, Jnne 20, 1900. P.S. Thort U 4 one word which you have misunder good in my former letter viz dißtioctive " which you have taken to be "lestruotive.'

Smart Capture by Superintendent Monaghan. On ?at uro ay morning the Warrington police re- ceived informition from the Oldham police of an extensive robbery of wearing apparel at Old ham by a couple of women. The same afternoon Superin- tendent Monaghan was passing Towns End when he noticed two women who he thought answered the description of the perpetrators of the robbery. He arrested them' and with the assistance of Sergeant Evans took them to the Police Station where it was found that they were the women who were wanted. Tney were wearina a portion of the stolen priperty and the other articles had been pledged in Warring- ton, but, were subsequently recover3d. The women were taken to Oldham and on Monday were each sentenced to a month's hard labour. WARRINGTON LIBERALS AND THE GENERAL ELECTION.

div.head: Mr. A. H. Crosfield the Suggested
div.p: Mr. A. H. Crosfield the Suggested
Candidate.

A special meeting of tfie general Council of the Warrington Liberal Association was held in the Committee-room of the Liberal Club, Beweey-street on Morida evening, for the purpose of receiving the report of the sub-committee appointed to consider the seleetien of a candidate to contest the Borough in the Liberal interests at the next general election, Mr. T Birhall, J.P., presided. • Prior to the commencement of the business, the CHAIRMAN said they could not proceed without paying a fitting reference to the death of the honoured widow of the great statesman whose name they all delighted to honour. The name of Gladstone weuld always be one of the greatest names emblazoned on the records of this country. Mrs Glad et me had been the honoured helpmeet of the late Or Gladstone for many years and no doubt contributed in Sonde degree to the great results which Mr Glaelstone achieved during his lifetink. He would like thY, meeting to express its regret at her death, and to instruct the secretary to convey their sympathy with the family of the distinguished stateemau. The suggestion was approved. the proposition being carried by ail present standing. The CHAIRMAN then eubinitte,d the report of the sub-committee with reference to the selection of a, cs.ndidate. It was pointed out that Mr. A. H. Croe- field had been approached, and it it were the wish at the party that ne should contest the Borough as the Liberal candidate he would do so. A discw,sion took piece, and the following reso- lution wes unanimously carried :—" That this meet- ing of the General Council having received the report of the sub-committee appointed to consider the sele,ction of a candidate to contest the Borough at the next General Election, approves their selec- tion and invitee Mr. Arthur 11. Crostield to address a meeting of the Council on a date convenient to himself."

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
CRICKET

Warrington have at last won their first match this season. The long awaited victory took place at Whalley Range and the team of that place were defeated by a majority of 66 runs. Houghton and Gibson batted in brilliant style for the visitors their respective innings realizing 32 and 25.3

The wicket was on the slow side, and consequently the ball always had the master hand of the bat. Whalley Range won the tcss and opened with C S Baker and H J Amos to the deliveries of E Connor and Thewlis. A disastrous start was made,and three wickets were down for eight runs, the initial batsmen failing to time the expresses of Connor, whilst the splendid length I...ain- tained by Thewlis caused scoring to be difficult. A G Baker batted ccnfidently And quickly added eleven, when a fine ball from the Warrington professional sent the home captain back.

Afterwards Butterworth hit freely until taken by Houghton at mid-on from a tall stroke, hut of the others none looked like making a stand, and the last three wickets fell at one total, 32. Thewlis came out with some remarkable figures, his seven wickets costing but 15 runs. kVarrington commenced with J Bibby and Thewlis, and both batsmen tried to force the game, the professional getting both Amos aud Butterworth away to the boundary. With eleven runs on Bibby was bowled, whilst at 14 a brilliant catch in the slips sent back Thewlis.

J Callon and E Connor quichly added 15 runs, when the fast bowler was sent back with eight to his credit, this number also proving fatal to Calton, who failed to get a thorough hold of one from Butterworth and was taken at mid-on. Disasters now befel Warrington in gulch succession, and nine wickets were down for 48, runs, T Houghton being joined by E Gibson. Botts batsmen played in confidout tity 10 placing both bowlers repeatedly to the boundary.

The fifty was ppeedily sent up by Houghton with a grand drive, whilst Gib.sou was applauded when he passed AMOS Eqoare for tour and three in SUCCOS3IVO strokes. With the total at 83 Saxelby and A. G. Baker took up the attack, and the aggregate had reached 98 before Houghton was caught at mid-on, having made 32 without a faulty stroke. His hitting all round the wicket was very fine, aPd needless to add both he and Gibson came in for a hearty reception on returning to the pavilion. Gibson'a 25 was free from blemish and his fearless hitting showed him to be possessed Of rare pluck.

The second eleven had Oughtrington Park for their opponents, the match being playel on the Arpley ground. Upson and Peterson opened the innings for the visitors. A disastrous start was made, two wickets fall- ing for one run. Bayliss joinei Peterson, making room for Whitelegge. At 68 Whitelegge was beaten by SFlcock. With J. Bolt in the soirteg bec tole much faster, the new batsman doing most of the hitting. The innings finished for 119.

Like their opponents, Warri,gton commenced very badly, R. Pierp .Unt being bowled after scoring a single, and Hawtin, who filled vaclncy, without scoring. Duckworth joined Silcock, and quite a different com- plexion was put on the game. The bowling was repeatedly changed, but to no purpose, and 100 was on the board before Duckworth was beaten. His score was made without a bleinih, and included three 6's, eight 42.4, and three 3's. Sileock also batted well for his runs. At the call of time Warrington had lost four wickets for 112.

Sankoy Wire NUN exp-rienced a severe defeat at the hands of Platt Bridge I.M. the respective totals being 72 and 23, For the winners, Battersby and Ratcliffe each c intributed a dozeLl runs, none of the Wire Mills players reaching doubie figures,
A rley Palk gaincd a victory over Walker's by a majority of eight runs. Then. was no scoring worthy of note, the totals being only 2/1 and 16 respectively.
Rylands Brothers succemied in disposing of Fairfield by the small maj rity of five runs. Crozier knocked up 13 for the winners.
Earlestown Wisleyans met St. Baroabas' on the ground of the latter team and sorle.eeded in defeating diem by 10 rune. F Clare scored 13 for the victors.

Cheshire Lines Engineers engaged Orford Barracks and defeated the soldiers by the respectable margin of 70 runs. For the victors Irvine and Brown batted in good style, scoring 19and 18 runs respectively.

Cheshire Line Juniora gained avietory over Glaze- brook the totals being 33 and 14. The bowfin?. of F Walker and Deeley was very praiseworthy, Walker taking five wickets for seven runs, and F Deeley taking five wickets for six runs. Walker performed the" hat trick."

div.head: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.
TUESDAY.—Before hil Honour Judge Gwynne James, and Mr. W. D. Joitiffe, the registrar,

ORDINARY BUSINESS —The number 'Of plaint cases before the Court was 57 ; defaitt summonses, ii;. ad- journed cases, 2 ; anti judgment summonses, 7. DISPUTE ABOUT THE SUPPLY OF MlL'—ln this Ca3e Ellen Davies, Hirdswood Farm, Aston-bv-Sutton, farmer, claimed £l6 19s 4d from Thomas Hill, Egerton-street, Runcorn, milk-dealer. There was a counter-alaim by the defendant for £33 us 6.1 which was alleged to be due to loss ,of basiness and profits consequent upon the plaintiff terminating the contract , without notice.—Mr. H. N. Linaker, solicitor. of IMessrs. Linaker and Linaker, Runcorn, appeared for plaintiff, and Mr. R. Swift, barrister, Liverpool, icntructed by Mr. Knowles, s ;Hefter, Widnes, for the dotence.—The c se was heard before the jury.—At the outset Mr.eSwift intimated there was very little dispute between the parties about the plaintiff's claim and the dispute only affected the milk item. Plaintiff claimed £l5 is 9d.and t'ney contended it should be £l4 16s 11d. As the history of the difference affected the counter claim, his Honour decided to hear that.—Tho mas Hill, milk dealer, Runcorn, said he was tho defendant. An agreement was came to between himself and the plain- tiff in November for the supply of 20 gallons of milk per day, and as much more as p-,Fsible up to 50 gallons. That bad gone on up to the 20th of March at which dates all the bills due had been met. From that date,. however, up to the 17th of April some dispute arose between the parties regarding the measure. On the 16th of Lpril, Arnold W. Davies, the plaintiff's son, visited the defendant's shop and presented a bill for payment. Defendant declined to pay it until it had been rectified, and the " shortages " taken off. Davies replied that he would have all the money, and that he bad got another customer so that defendant need not expect any more milk. The following day young Davies came again, and presented a further bill aed demanded the money. Defendant got sufficient money out to pay the bill, but would not do so until it had been rectified. Davies refused to do so, and left the shop. About three. quarters of an hour afterwards defendant received a solicitor's letter.—Thomas Hill, in the employ of the defendant, and the defendant's wife. Jane Hill, swore they were both present and could corroborate all that the defendant had said regarding the interviews. —Mr. Linaker intimated that the defence of the counter claim was a direct contradiction to the statement of there being an ageeement of a fortnight's notice—Arnold William Davies,, son of the plaintiff, said in November last he agreed on hie mother's behalf to supply milk to Mr. hill. All that had been said by the previous wit- mess regarding the fortnight's notice was untrue. Mr. Hill had never offered to pay any money but said " that he would not pay that day" and used most disgraceful language towards him.—Croes-examined : Witness admitted he did cell Mr. Hill " he would not supply him with any more milk unless he paid."—Edwin Bate, a farmer, swore he was present at the interview between the parties, and that Mr. Daviesi's account of it was the correct one.—Counsel having addressed the Jury, his Honour put the following ques- tions to them :—(11 "was Davis's Bill of the 17th April a correct one ?" (2) "Whether they could find if tbere was an agreement between the parties that the contract was to be terminated by either party subject to a fort- night's notice ?"—The Jury replied to the first in the affirmative, and to the second in the negative.—Hia Honcur accordingly entered judgment for the plaintiff on the claim £l5 10; and also en the counter-claim. —Mr. Swift applied for a new trial, but his Honour refused the application.
-,,ii0,--. Sudden Death of Mr. Joseph Dobson.

Vie regret to announce the death ot Mr. Joseph Dobson, of Froghall-lane, which occurred suddenly at his residence early on Wednesday morning. The deceased gentleman, who for 35 years had been en- gaged as a draughtsman in the Dallam office of Messrs Pearson and Knowles, was at the office on Tuesday, and although he complained during the day of an irregular beating of the heart he remained at his work until six o'clock. Ile was taken suddenly ill during the night, and died as stated. Dr. Nuttall had been attending him, and is able to certify the cause of death as heart disease. The deceased gentleman was 60 years of age. He was a native of Cumberland.and came to Warrington from the Loco Works, Whitehaven, in 1865, having been 'engaged by Messrs. Pearson and Knowles as chief draughtsman. His assiduity and ability won the confidence of his employers, and he continued in the office uninterruptedly until his death. He was an old member of the Conservative Association, having been associated with the party from the time the club premises were in academy-street. He was also a Freemason,and a Past Master of the 1,250 Gilbert Greenall Lodge.

div.head: WARRINGTON INFIRMARY AND DISPENSARY.
div.p: WARRINGTON INFIRMARY AND DISPENSARY.

A special effort is now being made to clear off the deficiency in the revenue account of the Warring- ton Infirtnary and the following letter has been issued :—" Dear Sir,--As President of the Warring- ton Hospital may I very earnestly ask your kind hell, either in toe shape of annual subscription or donation towards the funds of the institution. It embraces a large arei in Lancashire and Cheshire being about equi-Oistant from Manchester Liver- pool and Chester but too far from eacb to overlao their sphere of work. The annual report accom- panying this letter will I hope be sufficient evi- dence of the scope of the work and tke assistance rendered. Our hospital is free to all the poor and needy requiring help and you will notice that n, fewer than 7,000 persons availed themselves of it in One way or another in the past year. This town and neighbourhocd are increasing rapidly in popula- tion year by year and the need of the hospital is prooortionately greater. You wi I notice that the workingmen of Warrington through thkir own com- mittees have contribute,' as much as £624 and £679 in the last 2 years vsnectively. I much hope that many of our neighbours in Lancashire and Cheshire will join with our friends in Warrington and add tt eir names to the annual eubsc7iption list when the needs of our Institution, and the gooi work it is doing in their vicinity is brought prominently before them, awl thus help to reduce the annual deficit and pay off the accumulating debt which threatens to cripple its usefulnets —Yours faith- fully, J. CHARLTON PARR.
P.S.—Subicriptions may be paid Warrington Flovital Fund at Parr. 6 Bank. Warrington, or any of its branchen ; or to the ton. treasurer, George Dakin, Erg., Arlington House, Latchford, Warring- ton.'

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS.
Buller's Advance in the Transvaal. One Boer Shoots Another.

A Central News telegram from headquarters, Zandspruit, says :—Our column reached there to-day. One hundred and eighty-seven burghers surrendered at Volksrust, and many more would have surrendered had our line of march been on a north-easterly direction, so as to afford protection to those who laid down their arms. As matters stand many are afraid to deliver up their rifles for fear of reprisals from their own country- men. There are still a number of irrecon- cilables hanging upon our line of march. One typical incident will show the bitter feeling prevailing amongst them. The son of Com- mandant Woolman proceeded to a Boer com- mando and etronglf advised him to surrender to save useless bloodshed. He was promptly fired upon by a Boer named Coetzee, the bullet passing through his leg and killing his horse.

div.head: Widnes Victim of the War.
div.p: A Widnes Victim of the War.

Mr C. R. Teller, son of Mr C. B. Toiler. a Widnes manufacturer, who for a number of years has resided at Hawarden and been on most intimate terms with the Gladstone family. was Ann of the slain at the,battle of Heilbron. in South Africa. Young Mr Toiler was a trooper in the Oxfordshire Yoemanry, having joimd with several of his fellow-students at Oxford. With his father and the family the widest sympathy is felt, and the Rector of Flawarden (the Rev. Stephen Gladstone), hinrelf suffering under a similar grief, was one of th first to call upon Mr. Toiler and offer his condolences;

div.head: Warrincton Militiaman at Norvals Pont.
div.p: A Warrincton Militiaman at Norvals Pont.

Mr. S. Healey, 2, Pierpoint-street, has received a letter from Corporal C. Gleave. who is serving in South Africa with the 3rd South Lancashire (Militia) Reeiment. In It the writer says :—"You will have to excuse the writ- ing because I am writing this letter on Southern Hill one of the hightest ironies in Norvals Pent. We have seen Boers miles away but there is no chance of them seeing us. These hills are those which the Boers had. They are nothing hut a lot of cowards to be driven out of them so easily. One mAn on the top could keep forty from coming up. It takes three quarters of an hour to get to the top and we are ready to lie down when we $7.11, After being 27 hours on outpost duty with only a blank.t to cover us we are sent to work in repairirg the bridge which the Boers have binwn up. There is a terrible lot of sickness hDre. At Naanwpoort'and Bloeminntein they are buryirg 40 a day A few men of our regiment have died and a great many are in hospital. It is not for want of taking care of them there are so many deaths. The nurses are as good as mothers to them. If a soldier were at home, his mother or wife could not look after him any better. There are plenty of provisions to be got, but we want a bank behind us. Every thing is top price. lam quite a teetotaler since r have been here, but it is not my fault I can tell you. Beer is is per gill and even at this price they won't sell it to soldiars. We are 800 miles up country, but I want to go another 800 so that I can see something before I come back."

div.head: Runcorn Volunteers in Action.
div.p: Runcorn Volunteers in Action.

The following letter has been received by Captain George F Ashton. from Sergeant F J Jearnck, of the Runcorn Volunteers. Emanated, May 18th, 1900. Dear Sir.—Finding I have an hour or two to snare I will try and let you know how we are faring. I have just had my dinner and was wondering how I was going to pass away the time when it struck me I might drop my old Captain a line. In a letter from my father he said you had received my letter from Capetorvn but I am afraid that was a poor one. You must know that since then we have had some ups and downs. We were nocamnerl at Capeown about eight days and from there we we's sent to Naaue,peort. I must tell von we did some heavy marches at the Cape. We used to do about 12 rnil.,a day in heavy marching order ane it b-lag se very hot and dusty it was very hard work. It took us nearly three days to go by train to Naauwpeort. We encamped there and we had rather an easy time of it, we did little else bat fatigue duty. There was a large number of troops encamped there, tiae Cheshire Mi'itia Reserves and details were next tn us. We were getting good rations and were pretty comfortable but of course we were asxinus to get to the front- After we bad berm there a little over a week we got orders to proceed to Norve/s Pont about five hours' ride. We were accom- panied by the Cheshires and several other detachments. Norvals Pont comprises a few huts and a station. Here we had more fatigues, as you see the railway bridge scress the Orange River had been blown up and every day three or four hundred men were on fatigue carrying stones and unloading trucks, etc. It was very tiring as it was very hot and we began to wonder how long we were there for. The river was very handy and we used to be able to bathe and wash onr clothes, but we soon got tired of this place and wanted to he meving. We had hardly been there a week when we got our orders to move and march to Ittnemfentein to the regiment. We started on Sunday. April Bth,with the Cheshire Militia and some Household Cavalry and I about 300 remounts. We marched eh- WI ten miles.and stayed at Donkers Spruit for the night. After marching I for three days we arrived at Sprinefonteie. I forgot to tell you that One of our wagons carrying our tents broke down so we had to leave them behind and sive t he sky for a roof. At this place the Cavalry left us and we had to find 50 men for a guard on a train going up and I they took them out of our Comneny. As it happened all Runcorn men were amongst them except me. I had not the luck. We started from there abent three in the afternoon and marched about seven miles. We were now escorting a convoy belonging to the headquarters of the Bth Division which was going to Edinburgh. I can't tell you much of the march except we had some very bad weather very wet, and it made it very uncle). f.. rtable at nights, as we had to sleep out ie the open. We lived on biscuits and bully and bought fresh bread whenever we got a chance. We arrived at Edinburgh on the Saturday after God Friday, and we had a day's rest on Easter Sunday. The convoy left us there but the General of the 9th Division gave us some pipes, tobacco, and cigars for escorting them an. We finishei the journly ourselves and arrived at Bloemfontein on the 19th and went iota the Reat Camp. We fount out there that the regiment was some 25 miles away at a place called Karereand so we eot off rum-, morning and reached a place celled Glen and rested for the night, only having another eight miles to go. which we did next morning (Saturday.) We were welcomed by the regiment and by the other half of our Company and Were soon at home, feeling none the worse for the march of about 140 miles. Here we had fatigues and entre-etc duty to do and preparing for the advance. The regiment managed to get 'some stores up and we got some luxuries such as butter, cheese, jam, etc. You would see by the papers that the advance began on the 3rd of May. We are in the 15th brigade and we advanced towards Brand fort. Our regiment waif the advanced guard, and when we neared Brandfort the scouts found the enemy on a large kopje. We advanced in skirmishing order and made for a smell kopje in between us, and the enemy. Just as the firing line neared it the Boers opened fire wi'h artillery and wrae'd have played great havoc amongst us if they had burst, ,1 but I expect they were made in Germany. My com- pany was every lucky as we were ordered to retire and take up a position on a small knede in the rear, and justl as we arrived there the shells fell thick and fast just where we had left. We only had a few more about us as our artillery soon began to I play on them and off they went, not waiting for the Infantry. We marched on to the kopje and I stayed there all night till Saturday morning when we started again and aid a big march of about We continued marching day after day from daylight to dark till we got to Zsnd River where we came up with the Boers again. We took up positions in the night and early neat morning the fighting commenced and I never SAW a finer sight in my life than when I saw infantry advancing across a plain on to a konje occupied by he Boers. The artillery fire was very heavy on both sides and increased as time wore on. All this time we were lying in some bushes and lots of shall s burst e'en:it us. It however came to our turn to advan-e We formed for attack and advanced by sections. We thought we were in for some hot work as there were some Boers on a kopje who had to be movel and we were for it. I shall not forget the sensation in a hurry es we advanced under the heavy Artillery fire, but oefore we got near rifi-. range a few shells from our guns upset them and away they went. We advanced abut five miles and then halted for the night, the firing ceroing about three in the afternoon, lap to now we are right for a bar to our medal and that is semetiiinte We are now PnelraDqi near Kronnstad. We fully expected a big fight here and were greatly surprised when we heard that they had fl iwn and our cavalry had entered the tewn. Wet arrived here last Sa'urday and were told we sheuld ee a day's rest and very thankful we were for that as we had done semis heave marching and felt rather knockrd up. It is now Friday and still we are here and a good rime we are heving as we have nothing to do We are waiting for supplies and then I expect we shall ,

soon be off again. I must tell :you that the Company is doing very well and I mast say that my section is doing grand and second to none in the Company. The health of the Company has been very good although we have left a few down country. Up to now our section have orly left two behind, one at Capetown to look after baggage and the other at Karee through sickness. I am glad to say the Runcorn lads and myself are getting on famous an.l manage to do our duty. We are counting on being home again by August. I expect we shall be too late for camp this year but hope to be able to be with you in years to come. You must excuse me for this rousth letter but it is the best I can send you. Remember me to all our old comrades and to Sergeant Callaghan. I mast conclude now, so with best wishes. I remain, yours truly, (Sergt.) F. J. JEACOCK, P. 8.—1 hope the young fellows at Hatton will culist in the Volunteers.
