PICNIC FROM VULCAN.

The fifth annual picnic in connection with the Vulcan Mothers' Meeting of which Mrs Coiling- wood is sponsor, took place on Monday in beautiful weather. Something like 30 women left the Vulcan about nine o'clock in the morning in wagon nettes, accompanied by Mrs Collingwood and Mrs W Thompson, and drove to Earlestown station. Here they took train for Liverpool, where they spent a short time viewing the shops and market, finally making their way to the landing stage, where they embarked on one of the Wallasey ferry boats for New Brighten, which was reached about IJ. o'clock. After a ramble along the sands, dinner was part:tken of, and the afternoon, through the kindness of Mrs. Norman, who until this year was associated with the meeting, they were able to spend in the Tower gardens, some of the more ventutesome essaying a journey up the tower. Tea was partaken of at 530, and the lc- tervening time up to 8 o'clock was spent in various way. The return journey was commenced at 8 o'clock and at 9.30 Earlestoma was reached. Wagonnettes met the train and the party were driven to the Vulcan, after spending what was unanimously voted the moat enjoyable day they had had, since the institution of the annual picnic.

VIADUCT %VOILES OFFICE 'STAFF PICNIC. The annual picnic in connection 4vith the office staff of the L3ndon and North Western Company's Wagon Works at Earlestown took place on Satur- day under very favourable conditions. The plac- chosen this year was Lancaster, and the head quar- ters the King's Arms hotel. A special saloon was requiAtioaed and in this the party numbering 20 were conveyed by the 11.5 a.m. train from Earles- town, arriving at -Lancaster at 12.58. A most sumptuous repast was providel by Mr Duxbury the landlord of the King's Arms, and the good things were thoroughly enjoyed, the catering being of the very bast. At 2.45, the party boarded a char- a-banc drawn by four lirrses, and a journey of 26 miles was commenced. The weather was delight- ful for driving, the sky being somewnar, overcast, and the country was seen in all its loveliness. Tne route lay t.hrouo. Slyne, Bolton-le-Sands, Warton Cragg, Caraforth to Zeatand Conyers. returning by way of ti-311-)..-, and Halton to Lancaster. The King's Arms %vas reached without mi2hap at about 6-45, after one of the most pleasant outings it had been the good fortune of the party to enjoy. An excellent knife and fork tea was awaiting the hungry travellers, and it is not too much to say that they did ample justice to the god things provided, the catering and attention reflecting the greatest credit upon Mr. Duxbury. After tea the toast of the Queen was heartily honoured, and one or two other toasts hav- ing been suitably acknowledged,the party dispersed For the 8-40 train. Earlestown being reached about 11-30. The arrangements were excellently carried out by Mr. T. F. Roberts, who officiated as secre— tary.

WARRINGTON AND NORTH WICH LIGHT RAILWAY.'
Scheme to be Revived.

It is stated that the Warrington to Northwicb Light Railway scheme, which was rejected by the Light Railway Commissioners,chiefly on the ground that no provision was made for the compulsory acquisition of land, is to be revived. Mr. R H. Scotter, engineer of the undertaking, which is designed to connect the tpivns named, as well as the districts of Barnton, Little Lei?h, and innington, states that it is his intention to carry both schemes to:success as speedily as possible, and it is only a question of the arrangement of a few details before they can be presented in their amended form.

div.head: MILITARY NOTES.
div.p: MILITARY NOTES.

Major Weston of the sth Battalion Kings Liver pool Regiment with headquarters at Warrington ha e been appointed a specialservice officer for duty in connection with the force designated for operat- ing in Ashanti. Major Weston who is well known in Warrington bears a very high reputation as a capable militia officer. Re has passed in all military subjects and also holds a Ilythe certificate. The new 3rd and 4th Battalions Liverpool Regi- ments are being rapidly increased in strength, and men from the depot at Warrington are being con tinually sent to join the new units. Recruiting in the Bth Regimental district is very good indeed and in spi.aP the fact that the exigencies of active service have necessitated strong drafts being sent to South Africa to join the let Battalion Liverpool Regiment there are plenty of men available for ser- vice in the 3rd and 4th battalions now being formed.

Captain and Hon. Major Honlden obtains promo- tion to the rank of Major, in the 6ch Lancashire Volunteer Artillery in succession to Major aud Hon. Lieut. Colonel Heywood who has retired. Major floulden joined the corps in June 1882 and became captain in 1888.

Captain J P Fraser will, it is anticipated be pro- moted Major in the 2nd Lancashire Engineer Volunteers at St. Helens. and becomes second in command of the corps. Captain Fraser is now the Instructor of musketry to the corps. He has passed the examination for promotion to field rank ; has passed in tactics and also qualified in signalling. He joined the corns in March 1890 and was promo- ted captain in 1893. The training of the Cheshire Volunteer Infantry Brigade at Salisbury Plain under Colonel Shering- ham the chief of the 22nd (Cheshire) Regimental district has been very successfully carried out and at no time in the history of the Cheshire corps have they had such facilities for carrying out so much useful work as they have engaged in at Salisbury Plain. The brigade has unquestionably had a thorou2hly practical field and every endea- vour was made to impart to all ranks of the Cheshire Battalions a knowledge of duties in the field. The work has been arduous no doubt but officers and men have worked well together with the result that the period spent at this important centre has proved most beneficial to all ranks and the leesous learned will not be easily forgotten.

div.head: Letter V to ibe COttor.
div.p: Letter V to ibe COttor.
A'Complaint from Orford Ward.

Sir,—Will you kindly allow me to intrude on the space of your valuable paper, to give ventilation to the fol- lowing o are the officials responsible for the keep- ing of our back streets clean. also, the cleaning of the gutters and gullies (or grids) ? The back of my dwelling is in a shameful condition and has been so for a long time now. I have refrained from making any clmplaint up to the present time, ex- pecting that the officials who are paid to attend to these matters would in time be able to clear the drains of the runhish and filthy accumulations, if only for sanitary reasens. Perhaps when fever has made itself felt in this neighbourhood, we may be treated with an investigation as to the cause of it.

Perhaps, also, some of the Councillors who" adorn" this " Ward," particularly those who retire next Novemb:r might be pleased with an opportunity to display their zeal for the ratepayers. If any of them would care to call on me, I will undertake to furnish them with sufficient material upon which to base their "maiden effort" in the public interest. Can anyone explain why it is we cannot have the street lamps lit in Orford-lane until after 11 p.m., when most respectable people are in bed P—Thanking you in anticipation, yours respectfully, _
M. FLINAGRAN.

div.head: EFFECT OF INTOXICATION ON PAUPERISM.
div.p: THE EFFECT OF INTOXICATION ON PAUPERISM.

The Richmond Union, Surrey, asked tho Board to support the following resolution Resolved unani- mously that the Guardians of this Union, being of opin- ion that a large proportion of the pauperism and crime of this country is due to the excessive consumption ot intoxicating drink, and that one of the most effective ways ,of checking such excessive drinking is to protect children from its injurious and evil influences while they are too young to understand or assist themselves, most respectfully urge her Majasty's Government to pro- mote such legislation as shall render it illegal to supply children under the age of 16 years with intoxicating liquors for consumption on or off the premises ; and h-reby instruct the Clerk to prepare a petition for pr,- sentation to the House of Commons accordingly, and that copies of this resolution be sent to the Prime Minister, the first Lerd of the Treasury and local mem- bers of Parliament."

div.head: GRANARY RANSACKED AT
div.p: A GRANARY RANSACKED AT
BURTONWOOD.
Warrington Men Fined.

At the Warrington Csuntv Pdttv 5393i0139 on WPdneg., day before Messrs. John White (in the chair), Joshua Ball and Ziba. Armitage, William Plinston and John El wards, of Warring,ton,were charged with committing wilful damage to the wheels and blades of a mowing machine, a set of scales, a quantity of iron spouting, a window frame and a plougt:, the property of James Collier, farmer. Brook Farm, Burtoo wood, to the extent of £4 153 on May 26th. Mr J. W. Kaowles prosecuted on behalf of Collier.and said that his client and his wife came home on May 26 h at 4-30. When they got into the yard they saw the defendants throwing some of Collier's goods into a cart. It was found that the defendants had inquired from prosecutor's nine year old son, whether his father and mother were at home, and the by said they were not. Defendants then went into the granary and began throw- ing out all the goods they could find, one thing in par- tinnlar being the wheel of a mov-riag machine. The wheel would, including carriage, cost roughly a soYereign. rho blades of the machine had been oiled and stored in the granary. The defendant threw them t the ground and broke them. They then found some scales, threw them to the ground and threw a 561 b weirtht on rho top of them. The scales would cost abost £1 13, 61 to replace. Defend ants then smashed the granary window and pulled some iron spouting from an outbuddinz. If Collier had been a little later in (alining home the men would have eot away. The maximum penalry was £5 with the option of two months' imprisonmert and he thought that the 111108- trates would be satisfied in the case that there was only one punishment they could ir.flict and that was the ex- treme of the law. A more audloiouq act he did not think one csmld contemplate. Defeni?aor, brought the goods into town as old iron, Plinston being a marine store dealer. Evidence was then called. Defendants stated that prosecutor sold the iron to thPm.

The Chairman said then wan a terrible record against botk of them.—Plinnton would tr. fined 40; and costs anewould have to pay thcavnount of damage. Edwards, whom thP magistrates c,nnidered had acted under Plinston's instructions. would h. fined in the costs.

CHINA.
No Official News of Admiral Seymour. Relief Force From Taku.

Proclamation by the Admirals. The Secretary of the Admiralty stated that the following telegram has been received from Rear-Admiral Bruce : TAKU (VIA CHEFOO), JUNE 21ST. There has been no communication from the Commander-in-Chief for seven days, nor with Tientsen for five days.; Allies hold Taku forts and Tong Ku securely, and they will advance for the relief of Tientsin when in sufficient strength Troops are expected from Hong Kong to- morrow, and 300 from ‘vei Hai Wei the day after to-morrow.

It is believed that fighting is crmstantly going on round Tientsin. Our garriswa there should be about 3,000 tnen. The following prwamation was agreed to this morning to be at once i,sued :—The ad- mirals and senior naval offiers of the allied Powers in China desire to make known t 3 the Viceroys and authorities of the coasts and rivers, cities and provinces of China, that they intend to use armed force only against " Boxers " and peoples who oppose them in their march to Pekin for the fescue of their fellow-countrymen. Fighting at Tientsin.-300 Boxers

Killed. The fighting at Tientein is reported to haue been very sever:, the insurgents getting within fifty yards of the Russian troops, who killed 300 of them with fifteen rounds of artill ,ry fire. The foreign settlement was assailed on tvr° sides, but the Russian force, numbering 2,00 q, repelled the attack. Further details of the bombardment of th° Taku forts show it to have been a sanguinarY affair, the carnage amongst the Chinese having been terrible. Death of Count MuraviefF.
A Reuter' s telegram from St. Patershurg says that Count Muravieff, the Russian Minister for Foreign Affairs, died suddenly yesterday morn- ing.

LONDON AND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY SPORTS AT LYIVIIVI. The 36th annual athletic festival of the Liverpool em- ployees of the 'London and Narth-Western Railway Company was held at Lymaa on Saturday, the four special trains carrying close upon 4,000 persons. The weather was not of the most favourable description, rails falling at intervals throughout the afternoon. Amongst those who attended the festival were Messrs. W Bingham (president), Thomas Shaw (vice-president), J Lafthouse ',chairman), P Gi!lies (hors treasurer), John Pringle, and W H Evans (han secretaries), T Perrin (Birkenhead), H J Kinsman, J Bibby, Captain Braith- waite, Messrs. R Knowles, Tongue, Flume, Wellington and several representatives of the Lancashire and York- shire and Cheshire Lines railways. The London and North-Western employees' (Birkenhead) brass band, under the direction pf Bandmaster J Heron, played an enjoyable selection of music during the progress of the different races. The prizss were distributed by Mr. William Bingham. The events resulted as follows: 120 Yards (youths under 17 : 1, 3 Parkinson; 2, C H Hale ; 3. One Mile: 1, G W Barris ; 2, J Sudden ; 3, E Evans. 330 Yards Consolation : 1, Cahill ; 2, Lawrenson ; 3, Taylor. A Lunatic Throws Himself into the Canal. On Monday morning, at the Warrington Occa• sional Court, before Mr. F. A. Frost, John M oody, of Latchford, working at Messrs. Richmond's works, was charged with attempting to commit suicide by throwing himself into the Ship Canal at Latchford, that morning -George Rowley, a carpenter, stated that at G. 30 on Monday morning he was near the Swing Bridge, Latchford, when he saw the prisoner on the Warrington side of the canal near the bridge. He turned his head for a man-lent, and on looking again he saw him jump into the water, He, with the assistance of Robert Thomas (bridge- man) and others got him out.-Robert Thomas said he was a bridgerean in the employ of the Man- chester Ship Canal Company. From something he heard, he went to the canal and saw the prisoner in the water. He threw a lifebuoy to him, which eventually he got round the prisoner's body, and ! with assistance pulled him on to the bank. He was ! unconscious. Prisoner was remanded. A doctor• who subsequently examined him, pronounced him to be a luna•jc, whereupon he was taken to an as Impudent Theft at Burterswood-A Chase on Horseback. Michael Lee, a labourer, living in. Warrington, was charged at the Occasional Court on Friday, with breaking and entering a dwelling-house in Burtonwood and stealing two shirts, the property or James Sampson,-Isabella Sampqon. wife of the prosecutor, who lives at Warburton's Villa, Burton- wood, proved the theft.-James Sampson stated that when his wife told him what had occurred he went after the prisoner on horseback. As he over- took him ha dropped a bundle, which contained the shirts He (prosecutor), took him to the Warrington Police Station.-Prisoner. who pleaded that he was in drink, and did not know what he was doing, was remanded until Tuesday.

RUNCORN NOTES. [By A CORRESPONDENT] Seeing the number of lives that are year after year ended by a pre:tiature fall into the canals which abound in and about Runcorn, one is con- wained to ask: How is it, that the canals are not treated in the same category as railways, and more perfectly isolated from the public? The "tale of deaths" is a long one, and year after year it grows. Young and old, and even middle aged circum- spect persons fall victims ; still, nothing is done ! Let us hope, however, that the future will see the enactment of the law, or laws, which will bring the deaths from " falls into canals" on a par with a number of persons killed by " falls on the railway lines." Nonconformistq within the district have just completed their Sunday School Centenary celebra- tions, and brought to a successful close "the biggest and most successful thing ever undertaken in the town." But. successful as has been the venture, there is one thing to deeply deplore, and that is the attempt to throw ridicule upon the whole proceed- ings, which the too ardent enterprise of a local tradesman through the medium oi a local news- paper has brought about. The combined production is an insult to a body of people whose traditions are made up of the histories of noble men and women who have harmed neither tradesmen nor newpaPer ; and whose only crime—a glorious one—is their zeal in religion. That there should cam- e a day upon which a paper issued ostensibly for the purpose of commemora- tion, could so far forget the laws of propriety as to bemean itself by the lending of its columns to the publication of a burlesque upon the very cause of its special issue, is to be deeply regretted. Let us, however, dism- iss that subject and come to something mere congenial. The sum which the Wesleyan body of the town set out to seek was £2,000; truly, a large sum, and by the way all' of the money is deQtin-d to be spent in the furthering of Sunday school work. Well, they have succeeded, and when all the subscriptions &c. are in hand. the happy treasurers will find themselves blessed with more than £lOO above the sum they set out to ob- tain. They have the heartlest congratulation of everyone.

Warrington County Petty Sessions. __— WEDNESDAY—Before Messrs. John White (in the chair) Joshaa Ball and Ziba Armitage. Uarrdoltimi.En SACX OF Coat.. -William George Daniels was summoned for a breach of the weights and measures Act by selling sacks rf coal which had not a metal label affixed to the top. -P.O. Callaghan stated that he saw the defendant delivering coal from a lorry in Spring Lane. Croft. There were 25 sacks, 13 of which were unlabelled -Fined 5s includirvr Costa. CRUELTY To A NORM—John Fctrersley was summoned for illtreating a horse on the Ist inst. by causing it to be worked whilst in an unfit state.-P.S. Brindle stated that at 3 45 on the date named he saw a lad In the employ of the defendant driving a chestnut gelding attached to a spring cart in Manchester-, oad, Poulton. The horse was very lame on both fore legs. particularly on the off fore leg. He saw the delendant the following day and he admitted that he knew the horse was lame.-In.p .ctor Brown said the horse was quite unfit to work.-Defeniant was fined 51 and costs. rarnaatGE CONDUCT CF A DRUNKEN MAN.—Peter Barlow was charged with committing wilful damage to certain windows and doors to the extent of £2 lOs the property of James Unsworth of Croft.-Mr Herbert Woods (Messrs Ashton and Woods) prosecuted and sal i that the defendant had been living in the house to which the damage was com- mitted hut lately gave up possession. He afterwards went beck in a drunken condition and eommeneei by kicking in the door. He then went into the house and smashed all the windows, briarkinz 60 panes of glass. He broke one or two other doors, and then put them in the varden on the too of some hay and set fire to them, The damage was estimated at 505.--Defendant was ordered to pay the amount of damage and the costs, BREACH OF CANAL RitourATioatts -John Waterworth was summoned for working the flat " Pioneer" by means of steam on the St Helens canal at Sankey without a license from the London and Noah-Western Hallway Company on the sth of May.-Mr Fenna prosecuted on behalf of the railway com- pany and stated th it the summons was taken out under the St Helens Canal Act of 1833 whlch provided that any person using or working a vessel by means of steam without a license should forfeit or pay a sum not exceeding £lO. The defendant had ben in the habit several:times of working the ft It op the canql by steam. The damage done to the embank- ment was becoming very serious and for that reason the company did not grant licenses. The man had been warned not to do it. The company did not prosecute in a Irindictive spirit but just to show that the practice must not be a'lowed to continue -James ORS., Inspector of Canals, gave evidence and a fine of 2311 and c sits was imposed. The Coal Traffic on the Manchester Ship Canal. Nearly 10,000 tons of coal are now shipped weekly at the Partington tips on the Ship Canal, which are situated almost mid way between Manchester and Warrington. The bulk of it is used for bunker pur- poses on the boatF; plying between Manchester and foreign ports, only a small proportion of it being exported for consumption abroad, Buenos Ayres taking a small proportion for gas making pur- poses. Mr Pickwick. the official in charge of the Partington tips. has informed the writer that the coal shipped there is not all Lancashire coal as is so often made out, some thousands of tons being dr wn every week from Yorkshire. Cheshire, Staffordshire, Derbyshire, and other Midland coal- fields. It is confidently expected that the total shipments from Partington alone this year will ex- ceed half a million tons.
